Suppose you were to enjoy in this world the highest degrees of bliss; this bliss of yours is troubled by two things: either you lose this bliss through death, or it is lost to you through what you are exposed to of the changes of life.

As for the Hereafter, your life there is extended without end, and the blessing there is lasting and does not cease. It is a blessing without limits, because it is in proportion to the capacities of the Bestower, the Mighty and Majestic, in an abode of eternity that is not touched by annihilation, and it is certain and reliable.

Which of them, then, is better? For this reason the al-Haqq subhanahu calls us to reflection and reasoning: (Look) at which of the two transactions is profitable, so trade in it and do not accept any substitute for it.

So the Hereafter is greater and mightier, and there is no basis for comparison between the bliss of this world and the bliss of the Hereafter. I recall that we once travelled to San Francisco, and they took us to one of the hotels, not to stay in it, but to view the splendour, beauty and displays of refinement and luxury it contained.

Indeed, this hotel was a sign of the signs of creativity and beauty. I saw my companions, who were among the notables of the people, dazzled and captivated by its splendour, and I said to them one sentence: "This is what humans have prepared for humans; so how about what the Lord of humans has prepared for humans?"

Thus the blessings of this world and the displays of beauty in it must stir in us longing for lasting bliss in Paradise, not stir in us resentment and envy. We must take from the displays of luxury and bliss enjoyed by others a means to faith in Allah, and elevate this faith with upright thinking. If what we see of luxury, progress, refinement and construction in this world is the work of an engineer or a worker, then how much more so if the Maker is Allah the Creator, glory be to Him and exalted.

And we must not overlook the difference between the bliss of this world, which humans have prepared, and the bliss of the Hereafter, which Allah the Exalted has prepared. The utmost that people have reached in the luxury of service is that you press a button and tea comes to you, for example, and you press another button and coffee comes from it.

This is a machine that responds to you if you interact with it, but however far these people advance and however much their industry progresses, they will never reach the point of presenting to you a thing the moment it occurs to your mind, because this is among the bliss of Paradise which the Creator, glory be to Him, has prepared for His righteous servants.

So, since this is the case, and we accept that the Hereafter is better and greater, there is nothing for you but to hasten and take the straight path, and to follow the way of your Lord by the shortest direction, which is steadfastness upon the method of the One God and adherence to it.

Because He, glory be to Him, gave you in this world, supplied you with the means and the necessities of your life, He brought you into existence from nothingness and supplied you from nothingness, even if you are a disbeliever. Then He prepares for you in the Hereafter the lofty ranks and the enduring bliss that does not perish and does not cease.

These are the grounds on which you ought, after them, to know Him, glory be to Him, to turn toward Him, to cleave to Him and to be in His company, and not to make another god alongside Him. For if you do, you will not find any of this bliss; you will find nothing but blame and abandonment in this world and in the Hereafter.

In the Resurrection you will be confronted with your Lord, the One who called you to believe in Him, and you disbelieved. ﴿And He found Allah with him…﴾ [24:39]. At that moment you will regret when regret will not benefit you, after the opportunity has slipped from your hands. And He, the Exalted, says: ﴿So you will sit down, blameworthy and forsaken﴾ [17:22]. Sitting here is not an ordinary matter; rather it is the most painful state a human being can come to, because a person sits only when he becomes unable to stand. In it is a sense of exhausted strength, as if he has fallen to the ground after his legs can no longer bear him and no strength remains in him for movement.

We observe, in the Qur'an's expression about this one whose strength has collapsed and who has come to a complete end, that it chooses for him the posture of sitting specifically, and did not say, for instance: "you will sleep," because punishment does not occur with sleep. In sleep a person loses awareness and so does not feel the punishment. Rather He said (fa-taq'ud), thus upright and gazing, suffering the torment, because the torment is not for the limbs and the matter, but for the conscious soul that perceives and suffers.

For this reason physicians resort to anesthetizing the patient before surgical operations, because anesthesia removes awareness so that he does not feel pain. Among this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah has preferred those who strive over those who sit back by a great reward﴾ [4:95].

And He said: ﴿And women past child-bearing who have no hope of marriage…﴾ [24:60]. Sitting indicates inability, and at the same time one does not find rest in sleep, so he is in continuous torment. In the realm of blame the poet said:

"Leave nobility, do not travel toward its goal; sit, for you are the one who eats and is clothed."

And His saying ﴿blameworthy﴾ [17:22]: because he has done an action for which people blame him.

﴿Forsaken﴾ [17:22]: from abandonment (al-khidhlan), which is the absence of support. The one most distant in a situation where no one supports him and no one defends him, for this reason He, the Exalted, says to these people: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not help one another? Nay, today they are submitting﴾ [37:25–26].

Having directed us to the great doctrinal matter, ﴿Do not set up with God another god, lest you sit condemned and forsaken﴾ (22), (Surat al-Isra') God, may He be exalted, wished to show us that belief ('aqidah) and faith (iman) are not complete except through action. It is not enough to know God and turn toward Him. You must also consider what He has obligated you to do and what He has charged you with. For this reason we often find in the verses of the Noble Book the combination of faith and righteous deeds, as in His saying, ﴿By time, indeed mankind is in loss, except for those who believe and do righteous deeds and advise each other to truth and advise each other to patience﴾ (1-3), (Surat al-'Asr). The benefit and fruit of faith is righteous action. Since you will walk this path, expect to face the people of falsehood, corruption and misguidance. They will neither leave you alone nor make peace with you. You must arm yourself with truth, strength and patience so that you can confront them.

Another proof that religion is not verbal affirmation alone is that the disbelievers of Makkah did not testify that there is no god but God. If the matter were only belief in one God and the case ended there, they would have said it and testified to it. Rather, they knew well that faith demands something, that behind it lies a practical responsibility, and that believing in God requires you to act according to His will and to follow His method.

From here they rejected belief in one God, and they rejected submission to His Messenger (ﷺ), who came to convey God's will to them and to transmit His method to them. The method of God is not sent down except upon a messenger who carries it and conveys it to people, as He said, ﴿It is not for a human that God should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or that He send a messenger and he reveals by His permission what He wills. Indeed He is Most High, Wise﴾ (51), (Surat al-Shura). And here is the first of the rulings in the method of God: ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him﴾ (23), (Surat al-Isra'). God, may He be exalted, preferred to address (Rabbuka, "your Lord") over the word (Allah), because the Rabb is the One who created you, nurtured you, and surrounded you with His blessings. This term is more conducive to hearing and obedience, since a person should feel shame at disobeying the One who has bestowed favor upon him and who is the possessor of grace.

﴿Your Lord has decreed...﴾ (23): The address here is directed to the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), because he attained the highest rank in upbringing and good manners, and this is true upbringing, since God Himself raised him and perfected his manners in the best way. In the noble hadith: "My Lord disciplined me and perfected my discipline."

Qada (decreed): its meaning is "judged," because the judge is the one who rules. It also means "commanded." Here it encompasses both meanings. God commanded that you not worship except Him, as a firm command, as though it were a binding decree and judgment. The word qada may also come in the sense of "created," as in His saying, ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens﴾ (12), (Surat Fussilat). It may come in the sense of "fulfilled his purpose from a thing," as in His saying, ﴿So when Zayd had accomplished his need from her, We married her to you﴾ (37), (Surat al-Ahzab). It may also indicate the end of a term, as in ﴿So when Moses had fulfilled the term﴾ (29), (Surat al-Qasas). And it may come in the sense of "willed," as in ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ (68), (Surat Ghafir). Thus qada has multiple meanings, but all of them combine to indicate a thing that is binding and firm, in which there is no deficiency. As for His saying, ﴿that you not worship except Him...﴾ (23), (Surat al-Isra').

Ibadah (worship) is obedience to a commander in his command and prohibition, so that you submit to him by carrying out the command and avoiding the prohibition. If he leaves you something on which there is neither command nor prohibition, know that he has left the choice to you and permitted you: you may do it or not do it.

Therefore, the disbelievers who worshipped idols, who brought them as stones from the desert, used tools and implements to carve them, and when they broke they repaired them, and when they fell they set them up again, while seeing how contemptible they were before them, to the extent that one of them saw a fox urinating on the head of one of the idols, and said, disapproving of the foolishness of those who worship them:

"Does a fox urinate on its head?
Surely he is humbled who has foxes spend the night on him."

When they got entangled in questioning about these gods, they said, "They neither harm nor benefit, and we only worship them so that they bring us near to God in nearness." But how, when worship is obedience to a command and avoidance of a prohibition? So by what did the idols command you? And from what did they forbid you? Then your speech is a lie upon a lie. And in His saying, ﴿that you not worship except Him...﴾ (23), (Surat al-Isra').

This is a style they call the style of qasr (restriction, exclusivity), which indicates that worship is restricted to God alone and affirmed for Him alone, such that no one shares it with Him. If the verse had said, "Your Lord has decreed that you worship Him...," then someone might say, "And worship another as well," because the door of coordination (ʿatf) here remains open and unclosed, just as if you said, "I struck so-and-so and so-and-so and so-and-so," using coordination in this way. But if you said, "I struck none but so-and-so," you would have closed the door of coordination.

Therefore the expression came in the style of restriction to say: confine worship to Him, may He be glorified, and withhold it from others. Then God, may He be exalted, moves us to the second obligation and command after His worship: ﴿and to parents, good treatment﴾ (23), (Surat al-Isra').

God, may He be exalted, has linked His worship with good treatment of parents in many verses. He said, ﴿Worship God and associate nothing with Him, and to parents, good treatment﴾ (36), (Surat al-Nisa'). He said, ﴿Say, "Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you: that you associate nothing with Him, and to parents, good treatment﴾ (151), (Surat al-An'am). And He said, ﴿And We have enjoined upon man goodness to his parents﴾ (8), (Surat al-'Ankabut).

But why did God, may He be exalted, link His worship with good treatment of parents? Do you want us to bring the first closer to the second, or bring the second closer to the first?

We say: there is no objection to both being together, because God is unseen, and belief in Him requires the exercise of intellect and reflection. But parents, for a human being, are a sensory reality: they are the direct secret of his existence. They raised him and provided all the needs of his life, and they are the source of tenderness and compassion.

Therefore, the nurturing and care of parents is perceptible, whereas the nurturing and care of God is rational. God's command to you to do good to your parents is evidence of the obligation to worship God alone, without partner. He, may He be exalted, is the One who created you; He is the first cause of your existence, He is your nurturer and the source of your care, and He is the possessor of grace upon you before your parents. Did your parents raise you with what they themselves brought into being, or with what God, may He be exalted, brought into being?

Therefore the right of God must be joined with the right of parents, and each of them must be taken as evidence for the other. We note that when the Truthful, blessed and exalted, commanded us to worship Him, He used the form of negation: ﴿that you not worship...﴾ (23), (Surat al-Isra'). That is, He forbade us to worship other than Him, may He be glorified. But when He spoke of parents, He did not say, for example, "Do not mistreat your parents," in the form of negation as before. Why?

They said: because the virtue of parents is evident and needs no proof, and needs no rational argument. Your saying, "Do not mistreat your parents," would make them objects of suspicion of mistreatment, and this is not applicable to them and is not conceivable from them. When you negate something from one who should not be described by it, you have slandered him. For example, if you negate from one of the well-known righteous people, known for piety and scrupulousness, the drinking of wine, is that praise or blame in regard to him?

Because you have not said, "So-and-so does not drink wine," unless people were thinking that of him. Hence they said: negating a flaw from one who does not deserve a flaw is itself a flaw. Therefore He did not mention mistreatment here, because it does not come to mind and is not conceivable from a child toward his parents.

Then, despite the favor and kindness parents have shown you, do not forget that God's favor upon you is greater, because your parents may give birth to you and then hand you over to others, but your Lord will never hand you over to anyone.

As for His saying, ﴿good treatment (ihsanan)﴾ (23), (Surat al-Isra'): it is as though He had said, "Treat them well, good treatment." So the verb was omitted and its verbal noun was mentioned for emphasis. As for His saying, ﴿If one or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them "uff" and do not scold them, but speak to them a noble word﴾ (23), (Surat al-Isra'): when God, may He be exalted, the Truthful, enjoins us regarding parents, sometimes the injunction comes unrestricted, as He said, ﴿And We have enjoined upon man goodness to his parents. His mother carried him with hardship and gave birth to him with hardship...﴾ (15), (Surat al-Ahqaf). And sometimes He gives a reason for this injunction, saying, ﴿His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness...﴾ (14), (Surat Luqman). Whoever reflects on the two preceding verses finds that the Truthful, may He be exalted, mentioned the cause of honoring parents and the grounds that required this honor. But these grounds are specific to the mother, and they never speak of the father's virtue. He said, ﴿His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness...﴾ (14), (Surat Luqman). Then where is the role of the father? And where are his efforts during the years of raising children? Whoever traces the verses on honoring parents finds a general ground that mentions the role of both father and mother together, in His saying, ﴿As they raised me when I was small﴾ (24), (Surat al-Isra'). But before the father raises, and before his role begins, the mother had the greatest role. Therefore, when the father and mother dispute before a judge over a child they have together, the mother says, "He carried him as a burden and I carried him as a weight, he nursed him with desire and I nursed him with aversion."

Therefore the Qur'an mentioned the grounds specific to the mother, because she bore them alone, without the husband sharing them with her, and because these grounds preceded the son's awareness, so he did not perceive them. It is as though God, may He be exalted, wished to remind us of the mother's virtue that we did not grasp and did not feel.

This is in contrast to the role of the father, which is perceptible and known to the child. His father provides everything he needs, and whenever he asks for something they say, "When your father comes." So the role of the father is known and needs no explanation. The verse here enjoined parents in the state of old age. Why was this state singled out over others?

They said: because parents in their youth and strength are not objects of humiliation or neglect, and there is no room for irritation or annoyance with them. They are in a state of strength and ability to face life. Rather, the opposite is true: we see children in this state drawing near to their parents, seeking their pleasure, so that they may gain from their goodness.

But the state of old age and the appearance of senility is the appearance of dependence, need and weakness. After having been a giver, he has become a taker, and after having been a provider, he has become a dependent.

Therefore, the Prophet (ﷺ), in the hadith of the "Aminat" and the "Maraghim": he was on the pulpit, and the Companions heard him say, "Amin." Then he paused for a moment and said, "Amin," and paused again, then said, "Amin." When he descended, they said, "O Messenger of God, we heard you say 'Amin' three times." He said, "Gabriel came to me and said: 'May he be humbled in whose presence you are mentioned and who does not send blessings upon you. Say: Amin.' So I said: Amin. And may he be humbled who reaches Ramadan and is not forgiven. Say: Amin. So I said: Amin. And may he be humbled who reaches his parents or one of them and does not enter Paradise through them. Say: Amin. So I said: Amin."

Therefore God, may He be exalted, singled out the state of old age, because it is the state of need and the state of weakness. For this reason one of the philosophers said: "The best marriage is the earliest." When asked, he said, "Because it is the only way to beget a parent who will support you in the childhood of your old age." He likened old age to childhood, because both are in a state of weakness and need for care and attention. The Truthful, may He be exalted, spoke truly when He said, ﴿God is the One who created you from weakness, then made after weakness strength, then made after strength weakness and gray hair...﴾ (54), (Surat al-Rum). So whoever marries early will have children who will help him and assist him in his old age. In His saying, ﴿If one or both of them reach old age with you...﴾ (23), (Surat al-Isra'), whoever reflects finds that the attribute of old age was not stated unrestrictedly; rather He qualified it with His saying, "with you" ('indaka). The meaning is: they have no one other than you to care for them, neither brother nor sister nor relative who will take on this task. And since you are the only one left for them, be equal to the responsibility and do not evade it, for you are the most entitled to it.

The goodness toward parents extends beyond life, through seeking forgiveness for them, fulfilling the covenant they made and were unable to fulfill, and likewise maintaining the ties of kinship that are only maintained through them, such as the relatives of the father.

(wa-ikhfid) : Al-khafd is the opposite of al-raf' (raising).

(janah al-dhull) : It is well known that a bird raises its wing and flutters with it when it wishes to fly, and lowers it when it wishes to show tenderness to its young, embracing them and feeding them.

This is a sensory image for us, which the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, calls us to take as a model, and to treat our parents in this manner: we show tenderness toward them and lower the wing for them, as a metaphor for obedience, tenderness and humility towards them. Beware lest you be like the bird that raises its wings to fly with them, haughty over others.

The Wise Shari'ah often gives us examples and models of compassion and mercy in birds, and makes them an exemplar for us, the children of Adam. Whoever sees the bird embracing its young beneath its wing and feeding them with regurgitated food sees a wonder, for the young cannot chew or break up food, and they do not have the saliva that would make their food ready and easy to swallow. If you are able to witness this scene, you will see the bird and its chicks huddled together in joy and happiness.

So, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the wing of humility﴾ [17:24] is a metaphor for submission and humility. Dhull may come in the sense of subjugation and dominance, and it may come in the sense of tenderness and mercy. He, exalted is He, says: ﴿O you who believe, whoever of you turns back from his religion, Allah will bring a people He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers, mighty over the disbelievers﴾ [5:54]. If the dhull here meant subjugation, He would have said "adhillah li-l-mu'minin" (humbled before the believers); rather the meaning is "compassionate toward the believers." In contrast: ﴿mighty over the disbelievers﴾ [5:54], i.e., powerful over them, dominating them. In another verse He, exalted is He, says: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him are severe against the disbelievers and merciful among themselves﴾ [48:29]. Because the Creator, glorified is He, did not create man merciful absolutely nor severe absolutely; rather He created in the believer a flexibility that enables him to adapt according to the situations he passes through. If he is toward the disbeliever, he is mighty; if he is toward the believer, he is humble and lowly.

We see the clarity of this matter in the biography of al-Siddiq Abu Bakr and al-Faruq 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. Al-Siddiq was known for gentleness, softness of heart and mercy, while 'Umar was known for firmness in truth, courage and strength. 'Umar often said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he confronted one of the obstinate opponents: "Permit me, O Messenger of Allah, to strike his neck."

When the wars of apostasy broke out after the death of the Messenger (ﷺ), each of them took a position contrary to his nature. 'Umar's view was not to fight them during this critical period in the history of the da'wah, whereas Abu Bakr saw fighting them and taking them firmly by the hand until they returned to the domain of Islam and submitted to the command of Allah, the Exalted. He said: "By Allah, if they withhold from me a cord (*iqal*) which they used to pay to the Messenger of Allah, I would fight them over it with the sword. By Allah, even if none remains but the crops."

This stance of al-Siddiq and al-Faruq came for a lofty wisdom: had 'Umar said Abu Bakr's statement, it would have been something natural attributed to 'Umar's severity and boldness; but it came from the compassionate-hearted man, al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, so that everyone would know that the matter is not severity for its own sake, but for the preservation and defence of the religion.

It is as if the situation itself shaped Abu Bakr, and demanded of him this severity which overcame the gentleness prevailing in his character. Thus He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾ [17:24]. So: the dhull here is the humility of humbleness and mercy toward the parents. But your own mercy is not enough; you must ask for them the greater mercy from Allah, the Exalted: ﴿and say, "My Lord, have mercy upon them as they raised me when I was small"﴾ [17:24]. Because your mercy toward them does not suffice for what they have done for you, nor does it return their favour; the one who begins is not like the one who repays. They did good to you first, and you do good to them in return. Therefore ask Allah to have mercy upon them, and to take upon Himself, glorified is He, the repayment of their favour on your behalf, and to show them mercy that matches their kindness to you. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿as they raised me﴾ [17:24]: "kama" may indicate comparison, so the meaning is: have mercy on them with a mercy like their mercy toward me when they raised me as a child. Or it may indicate causation: that is, have mercy on them because they raised me when I was small, as He, exalted is He, says: ﴿and remember Him as He guided you﴾ [2:198].

The word (rabbayani) includes within this ruling every one who raised a person, even if he is not a parent, because a child may be raised by someone other than his parents for any circumstance, and the ruling revolves with its cause, existing or absent. So if someone other than your parents raised you, they have the same rights as parents: righteousness, kindness, good treatment and supplication. This is good news for whoever raised a child that is not his own, especially if the one raising is an orphan or in the position of an orphan. In ﴿rabbayani saghiran﴾ [17:24] there is an acknowledgment from the son of the favour his parents have shown him and of a kindness that deserves repayment. After that, the Truth, glorified is He, concludes this ruling with a matter in which the son's treatment of his parents is shared with his treatment of his Lord, mighty and majestic.

Al-Sha'rawi, *Tafsir al-Sha'rawi* (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66), on surah 17, verse 25:

We have already discussed faith (iman) and hypocrisy (nifaq), and we said that the believer is consistent with himself, because he believes with his heart and his tongue. The disbeliever is likewise consistent, because he disbelieves (kufr) with his heart and his tongue. The hypocrite, however, is inconsistent with himself, because he professes faith with his tongue and denies it with his heart.

This verse calls us to speak about hypocrisy, because it is a phenomenon that accompanies faith in God. As we know, hypocrisy did not appear in Makkah, which confronted Islam, opposed it, and restricted it. Rather, it appeared in Madinah, which embraced the religion and through which it spread across the corners of the earth. Some may ask: how is that?

We say: hypocrisy is a healthy sign alongside faith, because only the strong are subjected to hypocrisy. Islam in Makkah was weak, so the disbelievers confronted it openly and did not feign to it. When it moved to Madinah, its roots grew firm, its strength increased, and the weak-minded began to be hypocritical toward the believers. Therefore, someone may say: how can this be, when God censured the people of Madinah and said of them: ﴿And among the people of Madinah are those who have become adept at hypocrisy..﴾ (verse 101) (Surah al-Tawbah). We say: the Qur'an has praised the people of Madinah in the highest degree, saying concerning them: ﴿And those who had settled the abode and [adopted] faith..﴾ (verse 9) (Surah al-Hashr). It is as if He made faith the dwelling place of those who settled in it.

﴿They love those who emigrate to them and do not find in their breasts any need for what they have been given, and they prefer [them] over themselves, even though they themselves are in privation..﴾ (verse 9) (Surah al-Hashr). If He then says: ﴿And among the people of Madinah are those who have become adept at hypocrisy..﴾ (verse 101) (Surah al-Tawbah), then hypocrisy in Madinah is a healthy sign of faith, because if faith had not been strong in Madinah, the hypocrites would not have feigned it.

From here, God placed the hypocrites in the lowest level of the Fire, because he infiltrates among the believers as one of them, lives among them, and knows their secrets, and they cannot take precautions against him. He is an enemy from within, difficult to distinguish. This contrasts with the disbeliever, whose enmity is clear, evident, and declared, so one can take precautions against him and be on guard. But why speak of hypocrisy when we are concerned with the worship of God alone and kindness to parents?

God, glory be to Him, wanted to give us a subtle indication that hypocrisy, just as it occurs in faith in God, also occurs in kindness to parents. We see some children who are kind to their parents out of hypocrisy, for show and for reputation, not out of sincerity toward them, or in acknowledgment of their virtue, or out of concern for them. To such people God says: ﴿Your Lord is most knowing of what is in your souls..﴾ (verse 25) (Surah al-Isra').

Because some children are kind to their parents while within themselves they pray to God to relieve them of them. The address came in the plural form, "your Lord," meaning the Lord of the son and the Lord of the two parents, because your interest is the same to Me. Just as I defend the father, I also defend the son, so that he does not fall into what has an unpleasant outcome. His saying: ﴿If you are righteous..﴾ (verse 25) (Surah al-Isra') means: if the condition of righteousness is fulfilled in you, He will reward you with the fullest reward. If it is otherwise, and you are not righteous or sincere within yourselves, then return soon, do not persist in being unrighteous, but turn back to God and repent to Him.

﴿Indeed, He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back [in repentance].﴾ (verse 25) (Surah al-Isra'). Al-awwabun (those who turn back often) are those who acknowledge their sins and return repentant to their Lord.

We have already explained that the legislation of repentance by God for sinners is a mercy from the Creator to creation, because if a servant commits an evil deed in heedlessness of his religion or conscience, and no repentance were prescribed for it, we would find this single evil pursuing him, causing him misery throughout his life, and even calling him to another evil, and thus society would suffer from it. Therefore the Creator, glory be to Him, prescribed repentance to preserve the safety and security of society and to enrich the aspects of life within it.

Then the Noble Qur'an widens the circle of close kinship, which is "the two parents," to a wider circle beyond them. After it has urged him to be kind to his parents, it draws his attention to what is connected to them of kinship.

Al-Haqq (Glorified is He) having urged man toward his parents, progressed the matter and urged him toward the kin of his father and the kin of his mother, saying: ﴿And give the near of kin his due﴾ [17:26]. "His due" (ḥaqqahu): because God Most High made it a right (ḥaqq) for the relatives, if they were in need. If, however, they were not in need, then giving between them would be a mutual gift, each relative making gifts to his relatives and they making gifts to him. And al-Haqq (Glorified is He) wants to spread in society the spirit of social solidarity (takaful ijtima'i).

Therefore, some of the jurists of al-Andalus, when a man withheld zakat that had reached the threshold (nisab), would order that his hand be cut off, as if he had stolen, because God Most High named it (ḥaqq). Whoever withholds from the rightful owner his right, it is as if he has stolen it from him. The jurists of al-Andalus took this course because they were in a land of luxury and wealth, so they were strict in this matter, since no one had an excuse in it.

Thus, when one of their caliphs came to al-Mundhir ibn Sa'id and said: "I have sworn an oath, and I wish to make expiation (kaffara) for it," he gave him a fatwa to fast three days. One of them said: "You have narrowed what is wide, for God has also prescribed for expiation the feeding of ten needy persons, or clothing them, or freeing a slave." Al-Mundhir replied: "Or does one like the Commander of the Faithful get deterred by feeding ten needy persons or clothing them? He does that daily for a thousand and more; what deters him is fasting." Thus they took the ruling by its spirit, not by its text, so that it would match the capacity of the caliph and have an effect in restraining and deterring him.

The word (ḥaqq) occurs in the Qur'an with two meanings:

The first: in His saying: ﴿And those in whose wealth there is a known right﴾ [70:24]. The "known right" is zakat. The other meaning is an unknown and undescribed right, which is voluntary charity and goodness, whereby you give to God voluntarily of the same kind of what He has imposed on you, as He said: ﴿Indeed they were before that doers of good. They used to sleep but little of the night, and in the hours before dawn they would ask forgiveness. And in their wealth was a right for the beggar and the deprived﴾ [51:16–19]. He did not say "known," because it is goodness and an addition beyond what God has obligated upon us.

Whoever is given this right must be happy with it and regard it as a gain, not a loss, because the world, as we know, is changing: it turns over its people. The healthy may become sick, the rich may become poor, and so on. So your giving today is a guarantee for you in the future and a guarantee for your children after you. The right you give today is the very thing you may need tomorrow, should fortune turn against you.

So: the right you pay today to its owners is an insurance for you in the future that enables you to face life with strength, facing life without weakness or frailty, and knowing that your right is preserved in society. Likewise, if you leave your children in want and need, society will take care of them.

God spoke truly when He said: ﴿And let those fear who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would fear for them; so let them fear God and speak words of rectitude﴾ [4:9]. Therefore, people who have risen and prospered, out of piety, do not give zakat money to relatives, but reserve it for the poor who are distant from them, and they give their relatives from their own private wealth as help and kindness. The "needy" (miskin) is one who owns property but it is not sufficient for him, as shown by His saying: ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to poor people who work on the sea﴾ [18:79]. As for the "poor" (faqir), he is one who owns nothing. Some reverse the definitions of the needy and the poor, and this is a mistaken understanding. And: ﴿and the wayfarer﴾ [17:26]: al-sabil is the road, and a person is customarily attributed to his city, so we say: "son of Cairo," "son of Port Said." If he is stranded on the road and circumstances have arisen that make him need aid and help, even if in reality he is a person of means and wealth, such as when his money is lost, he has a right in the wealth of the Muslims to the extent that it brings him to his city.

When the wayfarer asks for help, do not question him about the reality of his condition, for he has an obligatory right, so do not put him in a state of humiliation or embarrassment. ﴿And do not squander wastefully﴾ [17:26].

As He said in another verse: ﴿And give its due on the day of its harvest, and do not be excessive; indeed, He does not love the excessive﴾ [6:141]. Tabdhir (wastefulness, from badhr, "seed") is israf. It is a process carried out by the farmer, who takes the seeds he wants to plant and scatters them by hand over his land. If he is skilled at this process, you find him sowing the seeds at equal proportions, distributing them over the area to be planted, so that the distance between the seeds is equal. Thereby the crop thrives and gives the yield hoped for. But if he sows the seeds haphazardly and without order, you find the seeds at uneven distances: many in one place and few in another. This is what we call tabdhir, because it places the grains in an unsuitable position; they are few in one place and crowded in another, so their growth is hindered.

Therefore, al-Haqq (Glorified is He) preferred to express extravagance by the term (tabdhir), because it squanders wealth in other than its proper place, spending it whenever it happens without system, so one may give lavishly where it is not needed while withholding in what is necessary.

Thus: tabdhir is the spending of wealth on what is not lawful, or on what is not needed or necessary.

The prohibition of tabdhir here may mean the prohibition of tabdhir in giving: that is, when you give the zakat due, do not let the joy of faith carry you away so that you give more than is obligatory upon you; perhaps you hear people's praise and thanks and so increase your giving, and then afterward, when you are alone with yourself, you may regret what you did and blame yourself for this extravagance.

It may also be that the meaning is: give to the near of kin, the needy and the wayfarer, but do not squander in other matters; the prohibition here does not refer to giving, but to trivial matters in which wealth is spent without necessity.

The word (أخ) (*akh*, brother) has the plural forms إخوة (*ikhwa*) and إخوان (*ikhwan*).

**إخوة** (*ikhwa*) indicates brotherhood by lineage, as in the words of Allah the Exalted:

﴿And the brothers of Joseph came...﴾ (12:58)

It also indicates brotherhood of goodness, piety and God-consciousness, as in the words of Allah the Exalted:

﴿The believers are but brothers...﴾ (49:10). Among this usage is His saying about Lady Mary:

﴿O sister of Aaron...﴾ (19:28). The intended meaning is that Aaron was the brother of Moses, peace be upon them both, and between them lay a long span of time, approximately eleven generations. Nevertheless, the Qur'an called them "brothers," meaning brothers in piety and God-consciousness.

As for **إخوان** (*ikhwan*), it indicates that a group of people has gathered upon one principle, whether good or evil. It thus indicates gathering in goodness, as in the words of Allah the Exalted:

﴿And remember the favour of Allah upon you, when you were enemies and He joined your hearts, so you became, by His favour, brothers...﴾ (3:103). It may also indicate gathering in evil, as in the words of Allah the Exalted:

﴿Indeed, the wasteful were brothers of the devils...﴾ (17:27). It is as if the wasteful people have joined with the devils in one identity, one affection, and one set of evil qualities has united them.

Therefore: the word (إخوة) indicates brotherhood by lineage, and it may rise to indicate brotherhood of faith, before whose strength all other ties collapse. We mention here what happened at the Battle of Badr between two brothers from one family: Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, who had believed, emigrated to Madina and went out with the army of the Muslims to Badr, and his brother Abu 'Aziz, who was still a disbeliever and had gone out with the army of the disbelievers from Makka. The two brothers met: the believer and the disbeliever.

It is well known that Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr was among the wealthiest people of Makka. He would wear only the finest and softest garments and perfume himself with the most precious scents, to the extent that they called him "the pampered one of Makka." Then, after he believed, his condition changed, and he preferred faith in Allah over all that wealth and luxury. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then sent him to Madina to teach people the matters of their religion. At the Battle of Uhud, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw him wearing a sheepskin and said: "Look at what faith has done to your brother."

So what happened between the two brothers, the believer and the disbeliever? And which bond was stronger: the bond of faith in Allah, or the bond of lineage?

When the battle raged, Mus'ab looked and saw his brother, who had been captured by a Muslim named Abu al-Yusr. So he turned to him and said: "O Abu al-Yusr, tighten your grip on your captive, for his mother is wealthy, and she will ransom him for a great sum of money." Abu 'Aziz looked at him and said: "O Mus'ab, is this your advice regarding your brother?" Mus'ab said to him: "This one is my brother, not you." Thus the brotherhood of religion and faith is stronger and firmer than the brotherhood of lineage, and Allah the Exalted spoke truly when He said:

﴿The believers are but brothers...﴾ (49:10)

As for His saying ﴿brothers of the devils...﴾ (17:27): that is, the Truth, blessed and exalted, made them partners in one attribute, which is squandering and extravagance. If the wasteful person has been extravagant in spending and has placed wealth where it is not lawful and where there is no necessity, then the devil has been extravagant in disobedience. He was not content to be disobedient in himself, but extended his disobedience to others, misled them into it, and made it appealing to them. Therefore the Truth, glorified be He, described him by His saying:

﴿And Satan has ever been to his Lord ungrateful.﴾ (17:27) He is not merely a disbeliever, but (كفور) (*kafur*, "ungrateful" or "exceedingly disbelieving"), which is an intensive form of disbelief, because he disbelieved and worked to make others disbelieve.

Let us ask: who is meant by the "turning away"? The previous verses spoke of parents, relatives, the needy and the wayfarer, and turning away from these does not fit the context of the verse, because it would be turning away from obedience to God. This is shown by His words:

﴿Seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for...﴾ (Surah al-Isra', 28). So God is in your mind, and through this turning away you seek the mercy, provision and abundance of God. Therefore, the turning away here is not sin or disobedience. What, then, is the purpose of the turning away here?

We say: A relative, a needy person, or a wayfarer may come to you and ask for something that you do not have at that time, so you feel shame at facing him with a refusal, and you are embarrassed before him. What you do then is turn to your Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and ask Him for what will meet your need and the need of the one who asks, and that He make a way out for you from this situation.

The meaning is: "If you turn away from them out of shame and modesty at facing them, since you have nothing to meet their need, then in this state you turn to God to show you mercy that encompasses you and them."

As for His words, Exalted is He, ﴿then speak to them a gentle word﴾ (Surah al-Isra', 28), as He said in another place about this same situation: ﴿A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 263). Even in a case of refusal, the Muslim must observe good manners, must not hurt the feelings of the one who asks, must turn him away gently and kindly, must show modesty and humility, must not act arrogantly or superiorly toward him, and must remember God's blessing upon him in making him one who is asked rather than one who asks.

Therefore, good words and righteous deeds in such a situation are not enough if you only say, "I have nothing," for the questioner may accuse you of arrogance toward him, or of not caring for him, or of being indifferent to him. Here the role of the elevations of faith and of the generous disposition of the human soul comes into play, which raise its possessor to the highest ranks. Consider this elevation of faith in His words, Exalted is He, concerning those with valid excuses in jihad (struggle in the way of God): ﴿Nor is there blame upon those who came to you that you might provide them with mounts, and you said, "I cannot find anything to mount you on," and they turned back while their eyes overflowed with tears of grief that they could not find something to spend﴾ (Surah al-Tawbah, 92). This describes some of the Companions (sahaba) who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to go out with him to jihad and to place themselves under his command and direction. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) apologized to them, for he had no mounts to carry them to jihad.

So what did these believing men do? Did they leave, their state saying, "We have done what is incumbent upon us," and rejoice in what they had reached? No. Rather: ﴿they turned back while their eyes overflowed with tears of grief that they could not find something to spend﴾ (Surah al-Tawbah, 92). Thus faith elevates its people and raises its companions. If they cannot perform practical deeds, then they perform words; if they cannot do this either, then at least there is the emotional response that expresses the reality of faith, which causes tears of grief to flow because of the constraint of their means.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 17, verse 29:

Almighty Allah spoke in a previous verse about the wasteful (al-mubadhdhirin), and warned us against this trait. In this verse, Almighty Allah establishes an economic balance that preserves for the human being the soundness of his movement in life.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched, lest you sit upon yourself blamed and regretful.﴾ [17:29] The hand is customarily used for giving and bestowing. We say: "So-and-so has a hand (yad) with me, and he has countless favours (ayadin) upon me," meaning that his bounties to me are many, because they are customarily delivered by the hand. So He said: "Do not make your hand, which is the means of giving, ﴿chained﴾ (maghluulah), i.e., tied to your neck. When the hand is shackled to the neck, one cannot spend, so here it is a metaphor for stinginess and withholding. On the other side: ﴿nor extend it fully outstretched﴾. The prohibition here is against extending it entirely, so some extension is permitted, namely spending within the limits of need and necessity. Extending the hand is a metaphor for giving and bestowing. Thus this meaning meets the meaning of the one who squanders (badhdhara) and the meaning of "tabdhir" about which we have already spoken.

Tabdhir (squandering) means: one takes a handful of seed and extends his hand with it once, so that it produces a heap of plants that devour one another. This is the forbidden squandering. As for the other, the one experienced in the process of sowing, he takes a handful of grain and grips it somewhat, to the degree that allows the seed-grains to slip out one after another, at close and equal distances, which is sowing (badhr).

This is the limit of moderation desired by the Wise Law, and it is the middle course, and both of its extremes are blameworthy. This meaning has also come in the saying of Almighty Allah: ﴿And those who, when they spend, neither are extravagant nor are stingy, but are ever, between that, [justly] moderate.﴾ [25:67] i.e., balance and moderation.

So: do not extend your hand fully outstretched, spending everything you have, but rather some extension that leaves you something to save, through which you can elevate your life.

We have already clarified the wisdom of this moderation in spending, and we said: balanced spending enriches the movement of life, contributes to its growth and advancement, unlike gripping and withholding, which obstructs the movement of life and results in idleness, unemployment, stagnation in the markets, and a slump that corrupts life and impedes its movement.

So: spending is necessary so that you contribute to the turning of life's wheel, and spending must be moderate so that you retain something of your income with which you can rise and raise your material standing in the world of people.

The squanderer and the extravagant you find in his place, not advancing in life a single step. How could he, when he retains nothing? With this divine, wise guidance we ensure the soundness of movement in life, and secure social and individual advancement. Then comes the natural result of extravagance and squandering: ﴿so you sit blamed and regretful.﴾ [17:29]

We have previously clarified that the posture of sitting indicates inability to rise and confront life, and it is a condition that befits one who has been extravagant until he has nothing left.

The word ﴿so you sit﴾ (fa-taq'ud) conveys diminished movement in life, because the movement of life arises from standing up to it and moving within it. Therefore He said: ﴿Not equal are those believers who sit [at home] other than those who have a disability, and those who strive in the cause of Allah.﴾ [4:95]

﴿Blamed﴾ (malumen): i.e., one who committed an act for which he is blamed and reproached. The first to blame the extravagant is his children and family, and likewise the stingy miser, for both are blamed for their unbalanced conduct. ﴿Regretful﴾ (mahsuran): i.e., remorseful over what you have come to be in terms of destitution and poverty, or from the saying "a camel that is mahsur," meaning one unable to bear its load. Likewise the extravagant cannot elevate his life or shoulder its burdens and aspirations for himself and for his children after him.

So if you grip with complete gripping, you are blamed; and if you extend fully outstretched, you sit regretful, cut off from the aspirations of life that you are unable to bear.

So: both extremes are blameworthy, and entail an evil whose outcome is not praiseworthy, in the life of the individual and of society. So: what is the aim?

The aim is that a person walk in balance (qawaman) between extravagance and miserliness, as He said: ﴿And those who, when they spend, neither are extravagant nor are stingy, but are ever, between that, [justly] moderate.﴾ [25:67] The Qur'an sets out for us a decisive, moderate constitution that regulates the economic movement in the life of society. So extend your hand in spending so that you contribute to the turning of life's wheel and to invigorating buying and selling, but not fully outstretched; rather, retain something of your income so that you may realize your aspirations in life. Likewise, do not withhold and be stingy toward yourself and your children, lest they blame you and dislike remaining with you, and you become an idle member of your society, not interacting with it nor contributing to enriching its movement.

Almighty Allah, who is the Owner of treasuries that never run out, and who said: ﴿What is with you will end, but what is with Allah remains.﴾ [16:96] If He, glorified is He, gave all His creation everything they desire, that would not diminish anything of His dominion, as He said in the Hadith Qudsi: "O My servants, if the first of you and the last of you, your living and your dead, your present and your absent, and your humans and your jinn, were all gathered in one open plain, and each asked Me his request, and I gave each one what he asked, that would not decrease what I have except as a needle decreases when one of you dips it into the sea. That is because I am Munificent, Glorious, Generous; My giving is speech, and My punishment is speech. My command, when I intend a thing, is only that I say to it: Be, and it is."

Allah, whose treasuries never run out, gives His creatures in measure. He does not extend provision to them completely, nor does He withhold it from them completely. Rather, He extends it to some people and restricts it for others, so that the movement of life may proceed. For if Allah, glorified is He, extended provision and widened it for all people, people would become independent of one another, and boycotts would arise among them that would corrupt their lives.

The movement of life requires that the owner of wealth need work, and the owner of work need wealth. Thus people's needs meet one another, people complement one another, and every member of society feels his importance and his role in life.

We have already mentioned that the Truth, glorified is He, did not make one person a collection of talents. Rather, talents are distributed among all of creation. You have a talent in one field, I have a talent in another field, and so on, so that people continue to need one another.

The wealthy man, whose wealth may make him proud and arrogant toward people, is brought by Allah to need the least of the trades that he disdains to practise, and he cannot avoid it if he is to take part in the movement of life.

The Truth, glorified is He, does not want, in the movement of life, for people to show favour to one another. Rather, people's interests must be bound to one another through each person's need of the other.

So, if the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, does not extend provision to His servants completely, nor withhold it from them completely, but withholds and extends, then behind that lies a profound wisdom of Allah, the Exalted. For this reason He has chosen this moderation as a method for His servants, to organise their lives. The servant must be content with what has been apportioned to him in both states, and must proceed in the movement of his life in a manner suited to the provision that Allah has decreed for him. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And whoever has his provision restricted, let him spend from what Allah has given him﴾ (al-Talaq, 7). That is: whoever has his provision restricted, let him spend according to his means, and not aspire to what is beyond his capacity and resources. This is an economic principle that secures for a person comfort in this world and provides him with a sound livelihood.

May Allah have mercy on a man who knows his own measure. For what wearies people in life and makes them wretched is that you see a poor man whose provision is restricted wanting to live the life of one whose provision is expanded, and aspiring to what Allah has favoured others with over him.

Let us imagine, for example, two colleagues in the same workplace who receive the same salary:

The first is wealthy and living in comfort; he may take from his father in addition to his salary.

The other is poor, and may help his father with the family's expenses.

If the two of them enter a shop to buy something, the poor one should look not to his job position but to his own material situation and standing, and buy what suits him, and not covet to be like his colleague, for each of them has a capacity and means that he must not exceed.

This is the precise economic principle and the balanced faithful conduct. Therefore, whoever respects the decree of Allah, is content with what He has apportioned to him, and lives within its bounds without rebelling against it, the Truth, glorified is He, says to him: "You have been content with My decree concerning you, so I will raise you to My decree regarding you." Then He gives him and widens his provision after restriction.

We see this in life, and the examples are clear. How many people were in poverty and narrow circumstances, and when they were content with what Allah had apportioned, their lives rose and their condition changed to abundance and luxury.

The Truth, glorified is He, extends provision to whomever He wills and measures it out, for He, glorified is He, wants the human being always to place himself in the station of vicegerency (khilafa) on earth, and not to forget this reality and imagine that he is essential to it.

The utter loss is that a person forgets that he is Allah's vicegerent on earth and proceeds through the movement of life as though he were self-existent in the universe. You are only a vicegerent of the One who appointed you, sustained by the One who sustains you. So beware of being deceived, and beware of living at a level above the one Allah has decreed for you.

If you regard yourself as self-existent, the whole universe goes astray. For Allah, the Exalted, has made the world alternating, and has made it turns of fortune. He who is widened for today may be restricted tomorrow, and he who is restricted today may be widened tomorrow. This is one of Allah's laws concerning His creation, so that the delusion of independence from Allah may be crushed within the human being.

If Allah had granted a person wealth permanently, the universe would never have enjoyed the sweetness of saying, "O Lord, provide for me," and if He had granted him health permanently, the universe would never have enjoyed the sweetness of saying, "O Lord, heal me." Therefore the human being remains connected to the Bestower, glorified is He, needing Him and calling upon Him.

Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿Indeed, man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ (al-Alaq, 6–7). Need is what binds a person to his Lord and connects him to Him, glorified is He. So extending and restricting provision by Allah, the Exalted, has a wisdom. He does not extend provision to them completely, so as to give them everything they desire, nor does He withhold it from them completely, so as to deprive them and show them what they dislike, but He gives according to measure and due proportion, so that the movement of life may be set right, as Allah says in another verse: ﴿And if Allah were to expand provision for His servants, they would surely commit excess upon the earth, but He sends down in measure what He wills﴾ (al-Shura, 27).

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is ever, of His servants, Acquainted and Seeing﴾ (al-Isra, 30): because if the Truth, glorified is He, had not distributed provision in this wise distribution, the balance of the world would have been disrupted. The one for whom it is extended becomes independent of others in what has been extended to him, and the one for whom it is restricted rebels against the universe and bears resentment toward people, envying them and opposing them.

However, when everyone knows that this is by the decree of Allah and His wisdom, the created universe will remain connected to the Creator who fashioned it, glorified is He. In His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord...﴾ (al-Isra, 30) there is a subtle point: that is, your Lord, O Muhammad, and you are the most honoured of creation to Him, yet He extended to you until you gave as one who does not fear poverty, and He restricted from you until you tied a stone upon your belly from hunger. If this was his condition (ﷺ), then none of us should disdain it when Allah restricts his provision. And which of us has tied a stone to his belly from hunger?

After the Truth, glorified is He, had spoken to us about one branch of life, which is wealth, and laid down for us the method by which life is set right and by which a person proceeds in a manner that secures for him a dignified life and a happy existence, and guarantees him the advancement and aspirations he looks forward to, He, glorified is He, wished to speak to us about life in its origin. So He commanded the preservation of offspring and forbade killing them.

The connection between this verse and the one before it is clear, because the discussion is still about provision (rizq). The Creator, glorified is He, warns us: beware of bringing the matter of provision into your reckoning, because you did not create yourselves, nor did you create your children or your offspring.

Rather, the Creator, glorified is He, is the One who created you and created them, and He is the One who summoned you and them into existence. Since He, glorified is He, is the Creator and the One who summoned them into existence, He is the guarantor of the provision of all. So beware of overstepping your domain and poking your nose into this matter, especially when it concerns children. As for His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And do not kill your children, fearing poverty﴾ [17:31]: killing (qatl) is the taking away of life, and so is death (mawt). But there is a difference between them that must be noted. Killing is the taking away of life by breaking the structure, because the human being is composed of a structure that the Creator, glorified and exalted is He, built, namely the bodily organs, and then He gives it the soul (rūḥ), and life arises in it.

So if a person strikes another person on the head, for example, his brain may be damaged and his life ends, but it ends through the breaking of the structure in which life was, because the soul does not remain except in a body that has particular characteristics; if these characteristics change, the soul departs from it.

As for death: it begins with the soul's separation from the body, and then its structure is broken afterward, and its organs decay. Death thus occurs while the organs are still intact.

This matter is akin to an electric bulb that does not give light unless particular conditions are met: a generator or source of electricity, a conducting wire, and the bulb itself. If this bulb is broken, the light goes out. Why? Because you have broken something essential in the process of illumination. Likewise, if someone shoots a bullet, for example, into another's heart, that person dies and the soul departs from him, because you have broken an essential element of the human structure, and the soul does not continue in the body without it.

Therefore there is no punishment in the Sharia for death, by which we mean here natural death, which begins with the departure of the soul from the body; but there is a punishment for killing. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Cursed is the one who demolishes the structure of God."

For the life of each of us is a structure erected by the Creator, blessed and exalted is He, and it is His property; it is not permissible even for its owner to tear it down. Otherwise, why did Islam forbid suicide and make it disbelief in God?!

So: what is forbidden in the verse is killing, because it is the work of humans, not death. The Noble Qur'an clarified this matter in His saying: ﴿And Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers have passed away before him. So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾ [3:144]: so killing is other than death. Killing is an aggression upon the structure of another human being and its demolition. As for His saying: ﴿your children﴾ [17:31]: the term "children" applies to male and female, but it is well known in the survey of history that they used to bury daughters alive specifically, not sons. In the Qur'an: ﴿And when the buried girl is asked, for what sin she was killed﴾ [81:8–9]. Because in those eras they regarded males as support and a force in the struggle of life and its assaults of some upon others, and they saw in them pride and continuation. Whereas they regarded daughters as a source of shame, especially under poverty, want and need, for a wealthy man might then lure a girl toward something reprehensible concerning her honor. By this understanding the meaning returns to provision as well. As for His saying: ﴿for fear of poverty﴾ [17:31]: that is, out of fear of destitution. And "imlāq" is derived from malaqa and tamalluq (ingratiation), and both return to need, because a person does not ingratiate himself with another except when he is poor in what the other has and in need of it, so he flatters him in order to take what he needs. As for His saying: ﴿We provide for them and for you﴾ [17:31]: in this verse there is a subtle point that must be noticed and understood so that we may be able to answer the enemies of the Qur'an who accuse it of contradiction. The Truth, exalted is He, says here: ﴿for fear of poverty﴾: that is, out of fear of poverty. So poverty has not yet come; rather, it is a possibility of occurrence in the days to come. Provision is existing and facilitated, so the one who kills his children in this state is not preoccupied with his own provision but with the provision of his children in the future. Therefore the order came thus: ﴿We provide for them﴾.

First: because the child is born and his provision is born with him, so do not occupy yourselves with this matter, for it is not within your domain. Then:

﴿and you﴾: that is, the provision of these children takes precedence over your own provision. The meaning may also be understood as: do not kill your children out of fear of poverty, for We provide for you through them and because of them.

We are concerned to clarify this matter because the enemies of religion who probe the Qur'an for grounds of objection see a conflict or repetition between this verse before us and another verse which says: ﴿Do not kill your children out of poverty; We provide for you and for them﴾ [6:151]. To these we say: you have approached the Qur'anic style without the Arabic linguistic faculty in understanding it, for the style of the Qur'an is not a rigid craft; rather it is an eloquent style which, in understanding and reflecting upon it, requires taste and linguistic sensitivity.

If you approach the words of God with sound reception, you will find in it neither contradiction nor repetition. Neither is the first more eloquent than the second, nor the second more eloquent than the first; rather each verse is eloquent in its subject, for although the two verses resemble each other at a hasty glance, there is a great difference in meaning between them. The verse of al-Isra says: ﴿We provide for them and for you﴾ [17:31]. We have explained the wisdom of this order: "We provide for them and for you." As for the verse of al-An'am: ﴿We provide for you and for them﴾ [6:151]: one must note that the verse has an opening (ṣadr) and a closing (ʿajz), and one may not understand one without the other; rather one must combine in understanding the verse its opening and its closing, and the meaning will become straight and will free you from any difficulty. What these people did was look at the closings of the two verses and neglect their openings. Had the opening been the same in both verses, they would have had a case for what they pursued, but the openings of the two verses differ:

The first: ﴿for fear of poverty (khashyata imlāq)﴾ [17:31], and the other: ﴿out of poverty (min imlāq)﴾ [6:151].

The difference between the two expressions is clear: in the first, poverty does not exist, for fear of a thing is evidence that it has not happened, but it is expected in the future, and the one concerned is not preoccupied with his own provision but with the provision of those who will come from his children.

As for the second expression, ﴿out of poverty﴾ [6:151]: poverty is present and actually occurring, and the person here is preoccupied with his own provision, not the provision of the future, so it is fitting here that the parents be mentioned first in provision before the children.

Since the openings differ, the closings must differ too, so where is the contradiction then? There is also another observation in the noble verse: the prohibition is addressed to the plural: ﴿And do not kill your children﴾ [17:31]. The subject is plural and the object is plural, and we have said before that when plural is set against plural it implies distribution into individuals, so the meaning is: let none of you kill his child, just as the teacher says to the students, "Take out your books," meaning that each student should take out his book.

If someone says: the verse forbids a father from killing his child out of fear of poverty, but it does not prevent a father from killing another's child as a favor to him, and the other likewise kills the child of another as a favor to him. We say: No, for the meaning of the verse is that not all fathers should kill all children, so that the meaning extends to my children and the children of others, and this is what is meant by setting plural against plural. But if we said the meaning is: you do me a favor and kill my son for me, and I do you a favor and kill your son for you, this would not stand, because the opposition here is not plural against plural. As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, their killing is a great sin (khiṭan kabīran)﴾ [17:31]: khiṭʾan is like khaṭaʾ, meaning sin and a great offense. It comes with a kasra and with a fatha, as we say: "take your precaution (ḥidhr)," and "take your ḥadhr." The word khiṭʾan: the letters khāʾ, ṭāʾ and hamza indicate failure to hit what is right, but sometimes the failure to hit what is right is because you did not know what is right, and sometimes because you did not hit what is right though you knew it, yet you transgressed it.

So when a teacher corrects his students' mistakes during the school year, you find him explaining to the pupil what he erred in, then correcting this error, and he would not do so except after informing his pupil of the rule he follows; but the pupil may overlook this rule and fall into error. Here there is no objection to correcting his error and guiding him, for he is still in the time of study, learning, training and drilling. But the matter differs if these questions are in the end-of-year examination: the teacher indicates the error but does not correct it, rather he assesses it with the marks counted against the pupil, and the matter ends with success for the one who was right and failure for the one who erred, for by the end of the year binding rules have become his, which he must follow.

The word (khaṭʾan or khaṭaʾ) is derived from khaṭā khaṭwa, meaning movement by motion. If the right thing is the fixed matter upon which people have settled and agreed, and then you exceed it and move away from it to something else, this is the error, that is, the step that caused you to pass beyond what is right.

From it is His saying: ﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ [2:168]: because he moves you away from the fixed thing established in God's law. The fixed thing here is that the Creator, glorified is He, created man and honored him to be His vicegerent on earth, to cultivate it and dwell in it by the method of the Creator, glorified is He. So how would the Creator, glorified is He, make you His successor, and then you come to sever this succession by what you bring about of killing children, who are the seeds of life in the future?

Even if we adopt the view of those who held that "your children" refers only to sons to the exclusion of daughters, and we grant with them for the sake of argument that you kill the daughters and leave the males alive, what then becomes of these males when they grow up and seek marriage?! And how would offspring continue with males without females?!

Thus this understanding does not accord with the noble verse, for the prohibition here is against killing children, who are sons and daughters together. The Truth, glorified is He, described the error here as great, saying: ﴿a great sin (khiṭan kabīran)﴾ [17:31]: that is because it is an error from several aspects:

The first: that by killing you have demolished God's structure, and none demolishes God's structure except God.

The second: that you have cut the chain of procreation on earth and nullified the vicegerency God established on earth.

The third: that you have transgressed the instinct of tenderness and compassion, for your child is part of you, and killing him strips you of all meanings of fatherhood and mercy, and even of humanity.

Thus the Truth, glorified is He, has set for us what guarantees the survival of offspring and the continuation of man's vicegerency of God on His earth, by forbidding every father to kill his child, and forbidding all fathers to kill all children.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 17, verse 32:

After Allah, glory be to Him, spoke of what protects offspring and preserves the succession of God on earth, He willed to shield this progeny from being lost and to provide it with a dignified life. When one of us is blessed with a son or a daughter, he rejoices exceedingly, prefers it over himself, takes the morsel out of his own mouth to place it in his child's mouth, and strives hard to secure for it a comfortable life and a promising future. The poet spoke truly when he said:

"Our children are our livers walking upon the earth;
If the wind blows upon one of them,
My eyes refuse to close in sleep."

But this cooperative system, which Allah, glory be to Him, made the pillar upon which family life stands, quickly collapses from its foundation if doubt creeps into the father's heart concerning the parentage of this child. His life then turns into an unbearable hell and a bitter inner conflict that he can neither confront nor voice, because it is an attack upon his very self.

Therefore, Allah, blessed and exalted, warns us against this abhorrent crime, in order to preserve people's lineages for them and to reassure every father about the descent of his children from him, so that he tenderly cares for them and protects them, and finds the pains and hardships of life sweet for the sake of their comfort. He, exalted is He, says:

﴿And do not approach adultery...﴾ [17:32]

Whoever reflects upon the verses of the Noble Qur'an finds that when Allah, glory be to Him, speaks to us of commands, He concludes the command with His saying:

﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them...﴾ [2:229]

This passage concerns the rulings of divorce, for which Allah, glory be to Him, set limits and commanded us to stop at them and not exceed them. It is as if He has brought us up to this boundary, and what is forbidden is to go beyond it. As for prohibitions, He concludes them with His saying:

﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them...﴾ [2:187]

The prohibition here concerns intercourse with women during i'tikaf (seclusion in the mosque), and it is as if Allah, glory be to Him, wishes that we not reach the prohibited limit, and that there be a distance between us and it. So He said ("so do not approach them") that we may remain at a distance from the prohibitions. This is a necessary precaution, lest we come near the forbidden and fall into it.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever grazes his animals around the sanctuary (hima) is about to fall into it."

Allah, the Creator of man, knows him best, and He does not want him to draw near to what is forbidden, because it has a glitter and an attraction before which a person often weakens. Therefore He forbade him mere approach, and distinguished between the act and approaching the act. The forbidden here is the act itself, so why then did Allah forbid approaching it as well and warn against it?

We say: Because Allah, exalted is He, wishes to shelter your emotions in this particular matter, the matter of the sexual instinct, which is the strongest of man's instincts. If you hover around it, you are about to fall into it; so keeping away from it and from its causes is safer for you.

When the scholars spoke of the manifestations of perception and knowledge, they divided them into three stages: cognition (idrak), then affect (wijdan), then impulse (nuzu').

Suppose you are walking in a garden and you see a beautiful rose. The moment you look at it is called "cognition" (idrak), because you perceived its existence by the sense of sight, and no one prevented you from looking at it and enjoying its beauty.

If it pleases you and its sight delights you, and its love settles in your soul, this is called "affect" (wijdan), that is, the inner emotional response to what you saw. If you then stretch out your hand to pluck it, this is "impulse" (nuzu'), that is, a practical action.

So in which of these three stages does the Shari'ah exercise control?

The Shari'ah controls the stage of impulse and does not prevent you from cognition or from affect, except in this matter, "the matter of the sexual instinct," where impulse cannot be separated from affect, nor affect from cognition. These are interlocked and intertwined stages, such that the human soul cannot separate them.

So when a man sees a beautiful woman, this sight quickly generates admiration and inclination, then passion and a violent instinct that calls on him to stretch out his hand, and the impulse we fear arises. Here he either yields and answers the call of his instinct, and the forbidden occurs, or he restrains himself and continues to suffer the bitterness of deprivation.

The Creator, glory be to Him, knows the nature of His creation and what stirs and surges within them of feelings and sentiments. Therefore He did not only forbid adultery, but forbade everything that leads to it, starting from the glance. He, exalted is He, says:

﴿Say to the believing men that they lower their gaze...﴾ [24:30]

For if you perceive, you will find; and if you find, you will act. If you take your share of impulse, you corrupt people's honour; and if you abstain, you live repressed, suffering a passion you will not attain and for which you have no patience.

So: the safest course for you and for society, and the most protective of honour and sanctities, is that you lower your gaze from what is forbidden of people, so you spare their honour and spare yourself.

Yet this truth is often absent from minds. A person deceives himself with forbidden mixing, and when questioned he claims innocence and good intention, and takes from companionship to kinship or neighbourhood a pretext for association and familiarity, while he does not realize that he is deluded in all of this, and that his Creator, glory be to Him, knows him better and is more aware of his state. He only commanded him to lower his gaze because of the corruptions and harms that result from it, whether they return upon society or upon himself.

Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The glance is a poisoned arrow from the arrows of Iblis; whoever abandons it out of fear of Me, I shall replace it for him with a faith whose sweetness he finds in his heart."

From here we understand His intention, exalted is He, in His saying: ﴿And do not approach adultery...﴾ [17:32]. He did not say "do not commit adultery," because this crime has preliminaries that lead to it. So beware of placing yourself close to it, for whoever hovers around the sanctuary is about to fall into it. Disregard those who call for mixing and licentiousness, for falsehood, however high it rises and however many its followers, will never become truth on any day.

Beware also of what spreads on people's tongues, such as their saying "she is his paternal cousin," or "he is her maternal cousin," or "they were raised in one house," and other such false sayings that do not change the face of the prohibited in any way. For as long as the woman is lawful to you, it is not permissible for you to be alone with her. In a Prophetic hadith: "No man should be alone with a woman except that Satan is the third of them."

Thus: Islam did not forbid looking merely as looking, nor did it forbid seclusion in itself, but it forbade both because they are among the motives and causes of adultery. So His saying: ﴿And do not approach adultery...﴾ [17:32] is more emphatic in prohibition, more cautious, and safer than "do not commit adultery." A similar example is His saying concerning the prohibition of wine:

﴿O you who believe, indeed intoxicants, gambling, idols, and divining arrows are an abomination from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.﴾ [5:90]

Yet there comes forth to us one who says: "There is not a single verse in the Qur'an that forbids drinking wine..." Glory be to Allah! So which is more emphatic and more intense in prohibition: that we say "do not drink wine," or "avoid wine"?

"Do not drink wine" is a prohibition of drinking only. Thus, it would be permissible for you to buy it, sell it, manufacture it, transport it, and so on.
