His saying: ﴿And Shaytan promises them nothing but delusion﴾ (Surah al-Isra) means: he cannot deceive with his promises except the one who has heedlessness and negligence. From this comes "al-ghurur" (delusion): that is, he makes falsehood appear to you in the form of truth, and so they say, "غره" (he deceived him). You can never make falsehood appear to a person in the form of truth unless his intellect is deficient and heedless, because if he were reasoning and attentive, the truth would become clear to him from falsehood. Rather, you seize him when his thinking is unaware and his intellect is negligent.

Therefore the True One, glorified is He, often addresses us with His saying: ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ (Surah al-An'am), and ﴿Will they not then reflect?﴾ (Surah al-Nisa'), and He calls us with His saying: ﴿O people of understanding﴾ (Surah al-Talaq).

All of this is evidence of the importance of the intellect and an urging to use it in all our affairs. So when you hear something, pass it through your intellect first. What is the meaning of Allah asking this of us? And why does He always awaken in us the faculty of thinking and reflecting on everything?

There is no doubt that the one who awakens in you the faculty of critical thought and discernment, and calls you to observe and reflect, is confident in the quality of his goods, like the honest merchant who sells good cloth, for example. He displays his goods to you with confidence and invites you to examine them, and he may even light a fire to show you their quality and authenticity.

Had the True One, glorified is He, wanted to take us thus in ignorance and blindness, without insight, He would not have called us to contemplate and reflect.

Likewise, Shaytan does not promise you or adorn for you anything except when he finds heedlessness in you. But if you were alert to him and kept your intellect with you, knowing his tricks, he would not find a way to you. Among his tricks is that he adorns this world for the heedless and says to them: "It is an opportunity for pleasure, so seize it and take your share of it, for you will not live twice. Beware lest you believe in resurrection, reckoning, or recompense."

These are whisperings that only someone disposed to disobedience believes, and who awaits a mere signal, then obeys and falls prey to false promises. On the Day of Resurrection, Iblis will disown these fools and say: ﴿Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I failed you. And I had no authority over you except that I invited you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me; blame yourselves. I cannot help you, nor can you help me...﴾ (Surah al-Ibrahim, cf. Surah al-Isra).

Thus, in the two preceding verses there are five commands to Iblis: "اذهب" (go), "استفزز" (incite), "وأجلب" (rally), "وشاركهم" (share with them), and "وعدهم" (promise them). These commands are not for carrying out their content; rather they are for threat and to show his inability to stand against the call or to turn people away from it. The True One, glorified is He, was saying to him: do what you wish and plan as you will, for you will not stop Allah's call. Therefore He said after them: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, and sufficient is your Lord as Disposer of affairs﴾ (Surah al-Isra, 65).

Earlier we discussed the difference between *ʿibad* (servants of God who devote themselves wholly to Him) and *ʿabid* (slaves), and we summarized it as follows. The *ʿabid* is subdued to his master in matters of compulsion and overpowering, but rebels against him in matters of choice. The *ʿibad*, however, are subdued in matters of compulsion and overpowering, and they also surrender their own wishes in matters of choice to the wish of their Lord. They consent to be subdued to God in all their circumstances.

The Almighty has spoken of His servants and chosen ones, as in His saying: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility, and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace." (63) And those who spend the night before their Lord prostrating and standing. (64) And those who say, "Our Lord, avert from us the punishment of Hell; indeed its punishment is ever a torment." (65)﴾ (Surah al-Furqan)

So the servants of God (*ʿibad Allah*), who are His chosen ones and beloved, are those who went out of their own wishes for His wish, and preferred to be subdued to their Lord even in choice. Therefore they deserved this divine protection against the plotting of Satan, his whisperings, and his deception: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you shall have no authority over them...﴾ (65) (Surah al-Isra').

We have already discussed the plotting of Satan, of which God said: ﴿Indeed, the plot of Satan is ever weak.﴾ (76) (Surah al-Nisa'). On the Day of Resurrection, when he argues before his victims whom he misled and led astray, he will say: ﴿And I had no authority over you except that I invited you, and you responded to me...﴾ (22) (Surah Ibrahim). That is, I had no authority of compulsion by which I could force you into disobedience, nor any authority of proof and evidence by which I could convince you of it.

Then the Almighty says: ﴿And sufficient is your Lord as Disposer of affairs.﴾ (65) (Surah al-Isra').

The *wakil* (disposer of affairs) is the one who supports and aids. You say, "I entrusted (*wakkaltu*) so-and-so," meaning you trusted him to carry out all that you want for you. If there is among human beings someone you trust and entrust with your interests, then what of it when your *wakil* is God, the Mighty and Majestic? There is no doubt that if God is your *wakil*, He is sufficient for you, supports you, and aids you, and He does not make you need anyone other than Him, glory be to Him.

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿Your Lord is the One who drives the ships for you through the sea, that you may seek of His bounty. Indeed He is ever Merciful to you.﴾ (17:66)

"Rabb" (Lord) is the One who takes charge of your nurture: creating you from nothing, and sustaining you from nothing. His sustaining (qayyumiyyah) is a gift that embraces both believer and disbeliever. "Yuzji" (drives): al-izjā' is sending forth gently, little by little. "Al-fulk" (ships) refers to vessels; the word is used for the singular and the plural, and for the masculine and the feminine.

Among its occurrences is His saying:

﴿And the ships that run in the sea with that which benefits people...﴾ (2:164)

And among them His saying:

﴿He is the One who enables you to travel on land and sea; until when you are in ships and they sail with them with a good wind...﴾ (10:22)

Then He says:

﴿that you may seek of His bounty...﴾ (17:65): "Ibtighā'" (seeking) is the intention toward a beneficial thing sought from the sea, such as sustenance or other things, as He says in another verse:

﴿And it is He who subjected the sea, that you may eat from it fresh meat and extract from it ornaments which you wear...﴾ (16:14). The sea is thus a source of livelihood and sustenance, and a repository of great wealth from the bounty of God; therefore He says after it:

﴿Indeed He is ever Merciful to you﴾ (17:66). "Rahmah" (mercy) is the expansion of the flow of bounty from God. He who gave you the land with its goods has also given you the sea with its goods.

The earth on which we live is either land, called yābisah (dry land), or sea; and although the proportion of dry land on the earth is a quarter or a fifth, the remainder is a vast, wide sea teeming with God's abundant goodness.

The ways of travel on land are many and varied: you can walk or ride, and each means of riding is according to the capacity of the rider. This one rides a donkey, that one rides a car, and you can move in them from one place to another. As for the sea, one cannot move in it except by being carried on something. So it is from God's mercy to us that He made ships for us, a sign of His signs, which carry us over the surging water, and He holds them by His power, so that we are safe from drowning.

The first to build ships by revelation from God was Noah (peace be upon him); they were not known before him, as evidenced by His saying:

﴿And he was building the ship, and whenever a company of his people passed by him, they mocked him. He said: If you mock us, then we mock you as you mock...﴾ (11:38). The people had no familiarity with ships; Noah's ship was primitive, made of wooden planks and ropes. Had God not guided him to the method of its construction and directed him to its arrangement, he would have had no knowledge of this matter. That the Truth, glorified is He, guides us through one of His prophets to a vessel which enables us to benefit from three quarters of the earth is undoubtedly a mercy to humankind and an expansion for them.

Likewise, from His mercy to us is that He facilitated the development of this vessel over the ages. Whereas it once moved on the surface of the water by the force of the wind, using what is called the sail (qal'), by which the vessel is controlled, and by which the skilled captain (rabbān) can tack the sail (tasfīh al-qal', meaning, directing it toward the side he wants).

So wind was the basis of ships' movement; then scientific progress came, which discovered steam and machines, then electricity, and thereby it became easy for humankind to move ships over the surface of the water with ease and facility. Ship-building also developed over the ages, until we now see large multi-deck battleships, which indeed resemble mountains, in fulfilment of the saying of the Truth, glorified is He:

﴿And among His signs are the ships in the sea like mountains﴾ (42:32). That is: like mountains. It is as if the Truth, glorified is He, gives us proof of His knowledge of what the world will reach of progress, and what the shipbuilding industry will attain of advancement reaching the point of becoming like mountains. Otherwise, at the time the Qur'an was revealed, there were no lofty battleships like these; they came into existence only after Archimedes' principle, upon which these battleships are built.

Yet despite all this progress in the field of navigation, we must not forget that it is divine power that moves these ships and carries them safely over the face of the water. Humankind should not be deceived by what it has attained of knowledge and imagine that it has become master of the reins of affairs in the universe, for the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿If He wills, He stills the wind, so they remain motionless on its surface...﴾ (42:33). Wind is the basis of propelling ships. Someone may now say: if the wind stops, we use other forces such as steam or electricity. We say: you have taken "wind" to mean only air; but if you look at the word "rīḥ" and what it means, you will find that the meaning of "rīḥ" is absolute force of whatever kind, as evidenced by the saying of the Truth, glorified is He:

﴿And do not dispute, lest you lose courage and your strength (rīḥ) depart...﴾ (8:46).

So: rīḥ is absolute force. The meaning of "He stills the wind" (42:33) is: He stills the force that moves the ships, whatever that force may be: the force of wind, steam, electricity, or other forces. If He wills, glorified is He, all these forces are rendered inoperative.

(1) Zajā al-shay': it became easy and straight. And azjāhu: he drove it gently. God says: "Your Lord is the One who drives (yuzjī) the ships for you in the sea" (17:66), meaning: He pushes them and moves them gently over the water. [al-Qāmūs al-Qawīm 1/284].

The sea is a state of distress and a crisis from which one cannot escape if harm befalls one there. On land, the ways of escape are many, but at sea there is no deliverance except by the care of God. He, exalted, says: ﴿Until, when you are in the ships and they sail with them by a good wind and they rejoice in it, a violent wind comes upon them and the waves come at them from every place, and they think that they are encompassed, they call upon God, sincere to Him in religion...﴾ (Yunus, 22). Thus is man, even the disbeliever: when his devices fail him and he finds no way out, he turns to God, the true way out and the reliever of distress. Man ordinarily does not surrender himself and keeps clinging to hope of deliverance.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when harm touches you at sea, those whom you call upon vanish except Him...﴾ (al-Isra, 67). That is, the danger encompasses them with a violent wind or a high wave, they sense the gravity of the situation, and there is no rescuer for them but God. Even the disbelievers, in this situation, are truthful with themselves; they do not deceive themselves or lie to themselves. Though they believed in other gods and worshipped idols and images, in this straitness they turn only to God and call upon none but God, because they know full well that their gods do not hear or respond, and possess neither benefit nor deliverance for them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿...those whom you call upon vanish...﴾ (al-Isra, 67). That is, those whom you took as gods have gone from your minds and have disappeared from your thoughts. So they will not say here, "O Hubal" (an idol), because they will not deceive themselves and will not be swept along by their lies at this grievous time.

In this straitness they will not remember their gods, and these will never occur to them at all, because the mere remembrance of them would weaken their trust in God, who alone possesses deliverance and whom they ask for help.

We had already explained this matter with the story of the village barber-surgeon (halaq al-sihha), who undertakes the treatment of simple folk and claims knowledge and expertise. When his child falls ill, he hurries him to the physician, because if he deceives people, he will not deceive himself, and if he lies to them, he will not lie to himself.

Likewise, man does not sell himself cheaply. When dangers surround him, he turns only to God, because He alone is able to relieve distress and aid the one in need, even if he is a disbeliever, because He, glorified is He, is the One who commanded him to turn to Him and call upon Him. He says: ﴿Why, when Our might came upon them, did they not humble themselves?...﴾ (al-An'am, 43). So if they call upon Him, He hears them and answers them despite their disbelief and obstinacy, because they are His servants, His creatures, and His handiwork. How merciful He, glorified is He, is even toward one who disbelieves in Him!

Therefore the Lord of Might said in the hadith qudsi (a saying of the Prophet in which God speaks in the first person, outside the Qur'an): "The earth said: 'O Lord, permit me to swallow up the son of Adam, for he has eaten of Your bounty and withheld thanks to You.' And the heaven said: 'O Lord, permit me to drop fragments upon the son of Adam, for he has eaten of Your bounty and withheld thanks to You.' And the mountains said: 'O Lord, permit me to fall upon the son of Adam, for he has eaten of Your bounty and withheld thanks to You.' And the seas said: 'O Lord, permit me to drown the son of Adam, for he has eaten of Your bounty and withheld thanks to You.' Then He, exalted is He, said: 'Leave them to Me and to what I have created. Had you created them, you would have shown them mercy. They are My servants. If they repent to Me, I am their beloved; and if they do not repent, I am their physician.'"

God, glorified is He, has forgiven them for worshipping other than Him, for harming the Prophethood, and for standing against the call. He forgave them because He is their Lord, and as long as He is Lord, He is merciful. They humbled themselves before Him and called upon Him, but when He delivered them safely to land, they turned away, returned to what they had been upon, and denied the favor and the kindness. Therefore He, exalted is He, says after it: ﴿And man is ever ungrateful﴾ (al-Isra, 67). "Kafur" (ungrateful, extremely ungrateful) is an intensive form derived from disbelief, meaning one who greatly denies blessings. Would that he had denied the blessing of creation, saying that this is how he came about by the nature of things! Instead he denies a tangible, observed blessing whose peril he lived through and whose danger he suffered; then, when God rescues him, he turns away and rebels. This is the nature of man.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 17, verse 68:

So are these people, who turned away from God after He rescued them at sea, secure from the scheme of God on land? Is danger only at sea? Is God, exalted is He, not able to bring them down on land just as He brought them down at sea? God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Do you feel secure that He will not cause the side of the land to swallow you up...?﴾ (Surah al-Isra', 68).

As God, exalted is He, said concerning Qarun: ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home...﴾ (Surah al-Qasas, 81). You are not any further from this if God wills it for you. Although we say "the land is safety," this applies among ourselves; but if the command of God comes, no preventer will protect us from it.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or He will send against you a storm of stones...﴾ (Surah al-Isra', 68). That is: a wind carrying pebbles, which pelts you with them. Al-hasba' (hasba', small pebbles) are small stones, and it is a kind of punishment that cannot be repelled or turned back. Therefore He said after it: ﴿then you will not find for yourselves any guardian (wakil)﴾ (Surah al-Isra', 68). That is: you will not find anyone who will help you or ward off (punishment) from you. So do not think that the land is a safety with no danger in it... No, rather my danger is present, not far from you, whether you are at sea or on land.

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 17, verse 69:

This means: if He has delivered you from the danger of the sea, there is no room for feeling safe on land, because He, glorified is He, is able to make you taste His might on land, or return you to the sea once more and bring upon you what He brought upon you of distress the first time. So the meaning is: you were saved and so you felt secure.

As for His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Then He sends against you a violent wind (qasif min al-rih)...﴾ (Surah al-Isra', 17:69): al-qasif is that which smashes with violence and intensity, and it occurs only over dry land.

﴿...and drowns you for your disbelief...﴾ (Surah al-Isra', 17:69): that is, because of your disbelief in the blessing of God and your denial of His favor. He saved you at sea, yet you turned away and rebelled, whereas you should have acknowledged to God His kindness and confessed His favor.

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿...then you will not find for yourselves any avenger against Us in that.﴾ (Surah al-Isra', 17:69): "Tabi'" (follower) and "tabi'" (avenger) differ here. The tabi' (تابع) is one who follows you to do something to you, whereas the tabi' (تبيع) is one who continually pursues you and searches for you in order to take vengeance upon you. So the meaning is: if We do these acts to you, you will not find for yourselves an avenger who takes up your cause or avenges you. Thus you have no hope of a helper who supports you or a defender who protects you.

It is as if the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, is saying: I do not fear your reaction, whereas a person refrains from acting out of fear of reaction, and sits pondering at length: "If I strike so-and-so, his family will come and do such-and-such to me." But as for the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, no one is able to repel His vengeance or His punishment.

Is there any honour given to the children of Adam greater than that He prepared for them the means of their life before He created them? He arranged the universe for them and created things for their sake: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on earth﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 2:29).

So, everything in existence is subjected to you before you even came into being; for God Almighty's creation is either a servant or one who is served, and you, O human being, are served by all the kinds of the universe, even by the angels. Did not the Truth, glory be to Him, say: ﴿For him there are successive angels before and behind him, who guard him by the command of God﴾ (Surah al-Ra'd, 13:11).

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿By those who arrange affairs﴾ (Surah al-Nazi'at, 79:5). The whole universe revolves for your sake and at your service; it gives you continuous bounty that never ceases without any effort on your part. Therefore we say: it was incumbent upon the pure intellect to stand in contemplation and reflection, so that it might reach a solution to the riddle of the universe and be guided to the fact that there is a originating Creator. It suffices that I look at the signs of God which serve me, over which I have no power and which are not under my control: the sun, the moon, the stars, the earth, the air, the water, the rain and the clouds all give to me and sustain me without any power on my part over them. Is it not your obligation, in justice, to say: who prepared for me all these things which no one has claimed for himself?

So if a cry goes out from one of you, O human being, saying: "I am a messenger from the Lord who created for you all these creatures," it would be incumbent upon you to lend him your attentive ear to hear what he has brought, for he will surely resolve for you this riddle that has bewildered you.

We have already given an example of this: a man who was cut off from his routes in the desert until he was near to perishing, and then he found a table prepared with the finest food and drink. Is it not fitting that, before he stretches out his hand to it, he should reflect on how it came to him?

So, man was required to employ his intellect and thought upon the provisions of the universe which serve him and are subjected for his sake, while they do not follow his command nor submit to his power.

The scholars have differed in explaining the aspects of the honour given to man. Some of them said: he was honoured with reason; another said: he was honoured with discernment; another said: he was honoured with choice. Some said: man was honoured in that he walks upright, not bent toward the earth like the beasts. Others hold that he was honoured by the form of his fingers and their harmonious arrangement in a wondrous shape that permits smooth movement in grasping things. Others hold that he was honoured in that he eats with his hand, not with his mouth like animals. Thus each of them had a point of view on the honour.

And we have in this matter of honour a point which I wished the scholars would have noticed, namely: that the Truth, glory be to Him, created the whole universe with the word "Be" (kun), except Adam. He created him with His own hand and breathed into him of His spirit. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O Iblis, what prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?﴾ (Surah Sad, 38:75).

And He said: ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down in prostration to him﴾ (Surah al-Hijr, 15:29). The pinnacle of excellence and honour is that God Almighty created the father of mankind with His hand, as evidenced by the fact that God made the hand a point of attribution to Himself.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 17, verse 71:

I.e., on the Day of Resurrection. The one who calls (al-da'i) is the caller (al-munadi), and the people are those who are called. The calling of people on this day will not be by "so-and-so son of so-and-so." Rather, each group will be called by its imam, i.e., its prophet, and it will be said: "O community of Muhammad! O community of Jesus! O community of Moses! O community of Abraham!"

Then this general statement is elaborated: each group is called by the one who conveyed the message to them and guided and directed them, in order to encourage people to transfer the credit of knowledge from themselves to others.

Some of them said: "with their imam" means "with their mothers." Calling people by their mothers on this occasion honors Jesus, peace be upon him, first, and conceals the sins of the children of sin, second, so that they are not disgraced before all witnesses in such a situation. Then the Exalted says: ﴿Then whoever is given his record in his right hand - those will read their record, and they will not be wronged even as much as the thread in a date pit﴾ (Surat al-Isra'). The fact that he takes his record in his right hand is the glad tidings of good and the beginning of safety. He hurries to read it, and even boasts of it among people, saying: ﴿Here, read my record!﴾ (Surat al-Haqqah, 19). He is joyful over his righteous deed, which he loves to have people see. As for the Exalted's saying: ﴿And they will not be wronged even as much as the thread in a date pit﴾ (Surat al-Isra'):

Injustice (zulm) is that you take from the good of another what is not yours. Thus, if you have a deficiency in something you want to obtain, you obtain it by wronging. So what could deprive the Truth, glory be to Him, so that He would wrong creation? Rather, creatures are characterized by injustice, because a human being usually is not content with what God has apportioned to him, so he feels a deficiency and wrongs others. But Almighty and Majestic God is free of need from creation, so how would He wrong them? All they possess is a gift from Him, glory be to Him.

As for the meaning of (fatilan): the Truth, glory be to Him, customarily strikes examples in the Qur'an using what is familiar to the Arabs and in their environment. Among the familiar things of the Arabs is the date, which is their preferred food and the fodder for their livestock. From the date the Qur'an took the naqir, the qitmir, and the fatil, three things that you find in the date stone, and it used them to represent something tiny and small.

- The naqir: a small hollow on the back of the stone, like a dot.
- The qitmir: the thin, transparent membrane between the fruit and the stone.
- The fatil: a fine membrane resembling a thread in the inside of the stone.

So the meaning of ﴿and they will not be wronged even as much as the thread in a date pit﴾ (Surat al-Isra') is that He, glory be to Him, never wrongs people; He, glory be to Him, is exalted above injustice, however small it may be. In contrast to "whoever is given his record in his right hand," the verse does not mention "whoever is given his record in his left hand," as in the Exalted's saying: ﴿But as for one who is given his record in his left hand, he will say, "Oh, I wish I had not been given my record"﴾ (Surat al-Haqqah, 25).

In another verse He said: ﴿But as for one who is given his record behind his back﴾ (Surat al-Inshiqaq, 10).

This is the counterpart of the one who is given his book in his right hand. For his insight was blinded in this world, so he is blind in the Hereafter. And since this is so, there is no doubt that he is among the people of the left. The verses mention the cause once and the effect once, so that cause and effect meet; this is what is known as al-ihtibak al-balaghi (the rhetorical device of interlocking omission, in which each half of a pair is left implicit in the other).

It is as if the Truthful, Glorified One had said: whoever is given his book in his right hand, and reads it and takes pride in it, was not blind in his worldly life; rather he was a seeing, aware person, who was guided to the method of God and walked in it, so this was his end and this was his recompense.

As for the one who is given his book in his left hand, he was blind in this world with blindness of insight, not blindness of sight; for blindness of sight is the blocking of the seeing faculty from perceiving visible things, whereas the unbelievers in this world were seeing visible things around them, perceiving the material aspects of life. But their insight had been sealed, so they see no good and are not guided to righteousness.

We have said before that in order for a person to walk the journey of life upon guidance, he must have sight by which he sees material things, so that he does not collide with one stronger than himself and be shattered, or with one weaker than himself and shatter him. Sight, for both believer and unbeliever, is a gift of lordship (rububiyya) to man. But alongside sight there is another gift, a fruit of the gift of divinity (uluhiyya), which is given only to the believer, namely insight (basira): the insight into values that a person acquires from the method of God in which he has believed and whose guidance he has followed.

As for His saying: ﴿So whoever is blind in this [life] will be blind in the Hereafter and further astray from the way﴾ [17:72]: if his blindness in this world was blindness of insight, then his blindness in the Hereafter is blindness of sight; for insight is required of him only in this world, because by it he will know good from evil, and upon it action is based, whereas the Hereafter is not a place of action. Thus, blindness in the Hereafter is blindness of sight, as God, Exalted, said in another verse: ﴿And whoever turns away from My remembrance, indeed for him is a depressed life, and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾ [20:123-124].

And He said of them in another verse: ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, mute, and deaf﴾ [17:97].

But someone may say: there are other verses that establish for them sight in the Hereafter, such as His saying: ﴿until, when they see that which they were promised﴾ [19:75].

And His saying: ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and will know that they are going to fall into it﴾ [18:53].

To reconcile these verses and harmonize them, we say: for the unbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, in regard to visual sight, there are two states. The first, at the time of rising and the terror of the Gathering, they are blind, mute, and deaf, so that their bewilderment increases and their dread intensifies, since they are in this severe distress, not knowing what is happening nor where to flee, and they hear no word from anyone; thus they are in distress and bewilderment, knowing nothing. This is the state of visual blindness for them.

The second state, which is sight, occurs when the Truth, blessed and exalted, manifests Himself to the people of the station and unveils Himself, glorified be He; then the unbeliever becomes sharp of sight, so that he sees his place in the Fire. Here we must note that words of the language may be one word while the context differs. In His saying: ﴿And whoever is blind in this [life] will be blind in the Hereafter and further astray from the way﴾ [17:72], the word "blind" (a'mā) is one word, but in the Hereafter He said "further astray" (wa-aḍall sabīlan). Therefore, the blindness of this world must be less than the blindness of the Hereafter, just as you say: "This is good." The opposite of "good" is "evil." But if you say: "This is better than that," you have preferred the first over the second in goodness. Thus the word "good" either comes as a description, or comes as a comparative.

Of this is the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "The strong believer is better and more beloved to God than the weak believer, and there is good in each." The meaning is that the strong believer is greater in goodness. Thus the phrase ﴿so whoever is blind in this [life] will be blind in the Hereafter﴾ [17:72] is not a description, but a comparative, preferring the blindness of the Hereafter over the blindness of this world, that is, he is in the Hereafter more intensely blind. And as for His saying: ﴿and further astray from the way﴾ [17:72]: it is known that he was astray in this world, so how can he be more astray in the Hereafter?

They said: because his straying in this world could be remedied by returning to the method and coming back to the straight path, whereas in the Hereafter his straying cannot be remedied, for the time of choice has ended. Thus his straying in the Hereafter is more intense and greater than his straying in this world.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 17, verse 73:

This is another of their wicked schemes against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They were earnestly trying to turn the Messenger of Allah away from what Allah had sent him with. Once they said to him: "Leave our gods alone for a year, so that we may enjoy them and take the spoils that come with them, and let our land, that is Thaqif, be made sacred for us just as Mecca was made sacred." Another time they said to him: "Do not touch the Black Stone," and they prevented him from touching it until he touched their idols first.

The meaning of "kadu" (they almost) is that they came close, and approaching is not the same as doing. Approaching is the beginning of an action and a plan for it, but it did not happen. They came close to tempting you away from what has been revealed to you, but it did not occur, because their attempts were from a distance. They encompassed attempts to divert you from the religion, as when they said, for example: "We worship your God for a year, and you worship our gods for a year." The meaning of "liyaftinunaka" (to tempt you) is to divert you and turn you away from what Allah has revealed to you. Why?

﴿That you might fabricate against Us other than it.﴾ (Surah al-Isra' 17:73).

As the Qur'an relates about them in another verse: ﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it.﴾ (Surah Yunus 10:15). So the answer from the Truthful One, glory be to Him, comes: ﴿Say: It is not for me to change it on my own accord. I only follow what is revealed to me. Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾ (Surah Yunus 10:15).

And the Exalted said: ﴿If Allah had willed, I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made it known to you. Indeed, I lived among you a lifetime before it. Will you not then reason?﴾ (Surah Yunus 10:16). We notice in such a situation that the Truthful One, glory be to Him, bears the harm on behalf of His Messenger, and moves the matter from the Messenger's sphere to His own sphere, so that there is no enmity between Muhammad and his people. The matter is not from Muhammad but from Allah. He says, exalted is He: ﴿We know that what they say grieves you. But it is not you they deny; rather, the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah.﴾ (Surah al-An'am 6:33). So do not grieve, O Muhammad. You are regarded as truthful among them, but the matter is with Me. In this way, the Truthful One bears the situation on behalf of His Messenger so that the people do not harbor rancor toward the Messenger of Allah. Then He says, exalted is He: ﴿And then they would have taken you as a close friend.﴾ (Surah al-Isra' 17:73).

The "khalil" (close friend) is the friend between whom and you there is love and affection, such that each of you penetrates and permeates the other. From this is His saying concerning Abraham: ﴿And Allah took Abraham as a close friend.﴾ (Surah al-Nisa' 4:125).

From this is the saying of the poet:
"When we met, the longing exhausted its effort,
two close friends melting with anguish and reproach.
As if one friend, within the interior of his friend,
slipped in during the embrace and vanished."
When two close friends meet, each of them melts into the other, or permeates him and enters into him.

The meaning is: if you had conceded the method that came to you from Allah, you would have become a close friend to them, just as you were a close friend to them before, and they loved you and called you "the Truthful, the Trustworthy." Therefore, what put them in a state of hostility toward you is the method of Allah that you brought. If you conceded it or were lax regarding it, they would take you as a close friend. So do not be a close friend to them, but a close friend to your Lord who sent you.

(Lawla) is a conditional particle which, when it precedes a nominal sentence, indicates the impossibility of the answer (the consequent) occurring because of the existence of the condition. They call it the particle of "imtina' li-wujud" (the particle of prohibition due to existence). For example, if you say: "Lawla Zayd 'indaka la-zurtuka" (Had it not been for Zayd being with you, I would have visited you), then the visit has been ruled out because of the existence of Zayd.

If (lawla) precedes a verbal sentence, it indicates urging and exhortation, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Lawla jā'ū 'alayhi bi-arba'ati shuhadā'﴾ [Why did they not bring four witnesses for it?] (Surat al-Nur) [24:13].

The (lawla) in the verse entered upon a nominal sentence, because the (an) after it is verbal-source (masdariyyah), so the meaning is: Had We not made you firm, you would have almost inclined toward them a little.

Whoever contemplates this verse finds that it takes several precautions on behalf of the Messenger of Allah. It does not say: "Had We not made you firm, you would have inclined toward them," no; rather it says "you would have almost inclined," so it negates mere approach, while inclining is a remote matter, absolutely prohibited and inconceivable from the Messenger of Allah. Nevertheless, the Exalted reinforced this meaning with His saying: ﴿a little﴾ [17:74] (Surat al-Isra'): i.e., a slight inclination.

This indicates that his nature, ﷺ, even apart from revelation from Allah, is a sound nature by its disposition. If we imagine that he had not been made firm by Allah, what would have happened from him? Merely "kada" or "qariba" (he almost) would have inclined toward them a little. We say: approaching implies the beginning of an act, yet it did not occur, which shows that the Messenger of Allah has an independent self. The meaning of ﴿We made you firm﴾ [17:75] (Surat al-Isra'): tathbit (making firm) is preventing the one made firm from wavering, which is why we say to the one who is moving: "uthbut" (stay still).

The meaning of (tarkanu) derives from a person's "rukun" (leaning) on something he holds to and takes shelter in. People build walls to protect their property, and if a person shelters himself by a wall and leans his back against it, for example, he has protected only his back and is safe from someone coming from behind him. If he wants to protect all four of his sides, he must resort to a corner (rukn) and lean his back against the corner, so he is safe from the front, and shelter himself by a wall on his right and a wall on his left. So, rukun means that you go to a stronghold that prevents you from all your sides.

From rukun is the saying of the Exalted about Lot, peace be upon him, with his people: ﴿Had I but power against you, or could I take refuge in a strong support﴾ [11:80] (Surat Hud): i.e., I would seek shelter in it and resort to it.

In these verses, the True (Exalted) intends to remove resentment against Muhammad, peace be upon him, from the hearts of his enemies, because he, peace be upon him, was keen on guiding them and winning their hearts, and he would burden himself and impose upon it what it could not bear in pursuit of this aim. Among this is what happened when he left 'Abd Allah ibn Umm Maktum, who came to him asking, and turned away to the chiefs of Quraysh; for this his Lord, blessed and exalted, rebuked him because he burdened himself.

It is as if the True, blessed and exalted, says in this verse: O people, if Muhammad does not agree with you on what you wanted from him, namely to turn away from what was revealed to him from his Lord, then excuse him, for the matter is with Me and the making firm is from Me, and Muhammad bears no blame for opposing you in it, just as if you had a servant who committed some error, and you wished to take the responsibility on his behalf, so you said: "I am the one who assigned him to this and ordered him to do it; the matter is with me, and the servant has no fault in what he did."

(إذاً) — that is: if you had come close to inclining toward them even a little, We would have made you taste double the punishment of life and double the punishment of death. By this threat, Allah the Exalted removes the rancor of hatred from the breasts of the people toward Muhammad, and transfers it (to them) Himself, glory be to Him.

As for the meaning of ﴿double the punishment of life and double the punishment of death﴾ (Surah al-Isra, 75): al-Ḍaʿf (doubling) is multiplying a thing once more, i.e., making a thing twice as much. Tasting, in life, refers only to punishment, so the intended meaning is: We would have made you taste double the punishment of life and double the punishment of death. But why is the punishment doubled in the case of Muhammad, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him?

They said: because he is a great example and a model that people follow. This act is impossible for him and is not conceivable from him, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him. But on the assumption that it had occurred from him, the punishment would be doubled for him, as Allah the Exalted said concerning the wives of the Prophet: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clear immorality, the punishment will be doubled for her twofold, and that is ever easy for Allah﴾ (Surah al-Ahzab, 30). That is because they are the household of prophethood and the Mothers of the Believers, and they are an example for other women among the Muslims. Whenever a person's rank rises in the position of calling to Allah, it becomes obligatory on him to keep far from suspicion, because he will be an example in action; if he goes astray, he will not go astray alone, but others will go astray with him. Hence Allah intensified the punishment and doubled it for the Prophet and for his wives.

Allah the Exalted chose the expression ﴿We would have made you taste﴾ (liadhaqnaka), because tasting (al-dhawq) is derived from the sense of taste, which is the most widespread faculty in the soul. You see with your eyes, hear with your ears, and smell with your nose, but taste is shared by all the faculties. Then He, the Exalted, says: ﴿Then you would not find for yourself any helper against Us﴾ (Surah al-Isra, 75). That is: you would not find a defender who would defend you, or a helper who would help you, because your support comes from Me alone; so how could there be a helper for you besides Me?

Here also is His saying, exalted be He, ﴿kādū﴾ (they nearly), meaning: they came close. They do not dare to act, nor are they able to; the matter is merely closeness to the act. They would attempt to expel you, but you will not leave except by My command and My decree.

As for His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Surely they would have almost driven you out of the land﴾ (Surah al-Isra', 17:76).

Whoever is "istafazzahu" (was provoked, i.e., roused) has been asked to rise up and move lightly to action, as you say to your sluggish child: "Fuzz" (i.e., get up and stand). The intended meaning is that they urge you to leave ﴿from the land﴾, from Makkah, by harming you and troubling you, so that they might compel you to leave and make you unwilling to remain there.

The Quraysh of Makkah knew that his departure, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, from Makkah would bring them ease, and that it would prevent his being an example to their slaves and to the weak among the people who loved him and inclined to embrace his religion and believe in it. Then He, exalted be He, says: ﴿And then they would not remain after you except for a little﴾ (Surah al-Isra', 17:76).

That is: if they expelled you from Makkah, they would not remain in it after you except for a little while. This did indeed happen: a year after his departure, peace and blessings be upon him, from Makkah came the Battle of Badr, in which seventy of the chieftains of Quraysh were killed and seventy were taken captive. After the Messenger left Makkah, they did not enjoy its comforts or the leadership they had hoped for after his departure.

Al-Sha'rawi explains that what happened is a sunnah (a established way or practice) of Allah with regard to the messengers, as He said: ﴿And Our word has already preceded to Our servants, the messengers. Indeed, they would be given victory. And indeed, Our soldiers – they would be the predominant.﴾ (Surah As-Saffat). So it is as if they should take a lesson from the earlier messengers, and from what befell their enemies of the punishment of Allah. Allah sent the messengers, and they were denied, harmed and persecuted, yet Allah granted them victory and made dominance theirs.

And the sunnah is the custom and method that never fails and never changes; therefore He says after it: ﴿And you will not find any change in Our sunnah.﴾ (Surah Al-Isra). For the sunnah is not transformed or changed except by one who is stronger, who comes to alter the sunnah with another from his own side. So if the sunnah is from Allah, the Strong, indeed the Strongest, then He, glory be to Him, alone possesses this transformation, and no one at all can alter the sunnah of Allah. When He, glory be to Him, speaks, His word is the truth that no one can change, and no one can oppose it.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 17, verse 78:

After Almighty God spoke about the divine matters (al-Ilahiyat), calling for belief in them, and about the prophethood (al-Nubuwwat), calling for affirming them, and about the Resurrection (al-Qiyamah) and the obligation to believe in it and in what takes place in it of the reckoning by the books, He, glory be to Him, wished to bring us the fruit of this method and its final outcome, which is that the path of life be set straight for us and our movement within it be regulated.

This divine method came in the form of rulings (ahkam), and these rulings have fundamental pillars which the Prophet (ﷺ) gathered in his saying: "Islam has been built upon five: the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, the establishment of prayer (al-salah), the giving of zakat, the fasting of Ramadan, and the pilgrimage to the House for whoever is able to make his way to it."

So, these are the pillars upon which Islam is built. But what is the share of the Muslim from these pillars? If you reflect, you will find that we all share in the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and in prayer, because it does not fall away from anyone for any reason, and it is repeated five times a day.

As for the remaining pillars, namely zakat, fasting and pilgrimage, their conditions may not apply to everyone: the poor man is not obliged to pay zakat or to perform pilgrimage, and the sick person is not obliged to fast. So, we have pillars of Islam and pillars of the Muslim, which are: the two testimonies and prayer, and to these may be added zakat, fasting or pilgrimage. So when the Muslim performs all the pillars, the pillars of Islam and the pillars of the Muslim coincide.

You will notice in these pillars that the two testimonies suffice if you utter them and bear witness to them even once, while zakat, fasting and pilgrimage may not apply to you in their conditions, so nothing remains but prayer; for this reason it was made the pillar of religion (ʿimad al-din).

Prayer is the established, repeated obligation that does not fall from the Muslim under any circumstance, and in it is a declaration of loyalty to faith in God every day five times. It also encompasses all the pillars of Islam, because in prayer you bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah; instead of saying it once, here you are saying it several times in every prayer. This is the first pillar.

It also includes fasting, because you fast during the prayer, refraining from the desires of the belly and the private parts, and likewise from any act other than the acts of prayer, and from speech other than the words of prayer. So in prayer there is fasting in the broader sense of fasting.

In prayer there is also zakat, because the wealth you earn and purify comes from movement, and movement is a branch of time, and in prayer you sacrifice time itself, so zakat in prayer is, as it were, more complete. Likewise, in prayer there is pilgrimage, because you turn in it toward the Ka'bah of God and bring it to mind and before your eyes.

For this reason prayer deserved to be the pillar of religion: whoever establishes it has established the religion, and whoever destroys it has destroyed the religion. From here the prayer came first among these rulings, so the Exalted said: ﴿Establish the prayer...﴾ (17:78).

That is: perform it in full, completely, at its appointed times.

Prayer has a distinction over all the pillars of Islam, because all the obligations of Islam came through revelation to the Messenger of Allah except prayer, which was enjoined directly, indicating its importance. We have illustrated this, and to God belongs the highest likeness, by a head who calls his subordinate by telephone to order him to do something; if that matter is of such importance, he summons him to his presence and makes him understand what he wants.

So it was with prayer: it was enjoined upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and upon his community directly, because of its importance among the obligations of religion. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) took charge of teaching the Messenger of Allah the prayer, and the Messenger of Allah taught it to the people, and said: "Pray as you have seen me pray."

As for His saying: ﴿At the decline of the sun...﴾ (17:78): Almighty God wishes to explain to us the times of prayer. And "dulūk" (al-dulūk) means moving away from one motion to another; from it comes our saying of a person "al-mudallikati," meaning the one who undertakes the process of massaging, whose hand moves from place to place.

The meaning of the decline of the sun is its inclining away from the middle of the sky toward the west. A person sees the wide horizon when he looks at the sky, and he sees it in the shape of an extended arc; according to his sight and strength he sees the horizon: if his sight is strong he sees the horizon as wide, and if his sight is weak he sees it as narrow; for this reason they say of a narrow-minded thinker: "narrow horizon" (dayyiq al-ufuq).

When you stand in your place and look at the sky, you see it in the shape of a semicircle, with you at its center. When you see the sun directly overhead, this is the time of zawal (the meridian). When the sun inclines toward the west, it is said: "the sun has declined" (dalakat al-shams), meaning it has inclined toward the west, and this is the time of Dhuhr.

Whoever reflects on the obligation of prayer upon the Messenger of Allah finds that Dhuhr is the first prayer the Messenger of Allah performed, because prayer was enjoined upon him in the heavens during the Night Journey and Ascension (al-Mi'raj), and it was at night; so when he (ﷺ) returned, it was the time of Dhuhr, and so it was the first prayer.

Then He, the Exalted, says: ﴿...until the darkness of the night...﴾ (17:78): that is, establish the prayer at the decline of the sun until when? Until the darkness of the night, that is, its gloom. In the period from the decline of the sun to the darkness of the night fall the prayers of Dhuhr, 'Asr, Maghrib and 'Isha', and nothing remains for the Subh prayer. So He, glory be to Him, said of it: ﴿And the recitation of dawn; indeed the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed﴾ (17:78).

Here we ask: why was the recitation of dawn mentioned and not "prayer"?

They said: because the Qur'an at this time, when the world is still and souls are clear, is received fresh and moist, and is taken in with conscious reception before one is occupied with the affairs of life: ﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed﴾ (17:78), that is, witnessed by the angels. So witnessing has a bearing on worship. If the witnessing of those who are not under obligation in prayer has been made a reason, how much more the witnessing of those who are charged with prayer?

Almighty God has placed in congregational prayer a path to servitude: in congregational prayer all creatures are equal, as they set aside their rank and their stations at the doors of the mosque, just as they remove their shoes; the head of state stands beside the subordinate, and the minister beside the watchman.

For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade a person to reserve for himself a place in the mosque where he sits continually, because the principle is that the worshipper sits where the gathering brings him, so people sit by priority of arrival, each according to his place and his haste to prayer; no one steps over the necks of others, nor separates two people.

We see some worshippers hurrying to the first row, for example, and placing their prayer mat to reserve a place with it, then leaving for their need; when he is late for prayer he comes to step over people's necks to reach his place, and then people become annoyed at this conduct and move his mat aside and sit in its place. This is a conduct unworthy of the houses of God, which make all of God's creatures equal and realize the path of servitude to God. Today you are beside so-and-so, and tomorrow beside another; all are humbled before God, bowing and prostrating, so no one may exalt himself over anyone.

We also see the path of servitude clearly in the rites of the Hajj, where one of the great and notable men comes, and you see him at the Multazam humbled, abased, weeping and supplicating, though he is who he is in the world of people.

So the time of Fajr is a blessed, witnessed time, witnessed by the angels of the night, who are not under obligation to pray; and the better witnessing is that of the worshippers whom God has charged with prayer and made to benefit from it.

For this reason congregational prayer is better than individual prayer by twenty-seven degrees, as came in the noble Prophetic hadith.

We must notice that Almighty God linked the five prayers to time, and to a cosmic sign that indicates it, namely the sun. So what is to be done when it sets, or is hidden from us by clouds or the like?

So the believing person must strive and apply his thinking to find something by which to regulate his time, and indeed human ingenuity has produced the instruments of time-keeping existing now, which greatly facilitate matters for people. Therefore, the human aspirations toward things that serve religion and clarify its features are a duty upon the scholars of the Muslims, on the principle that what a obligation cannot be completed without is itself obligatory.

Al-Hujud (الهجود): it is sleep, and tahajjud (تهجد) means that he removed sleep and lethargy from himself. This is a special privilege of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and an addition to what was obligated upon his ummah: that he stand in worship to Allah during the night, as his Lord, exalted is He, said to him: ﴿O you who wraps himself (in garments)! Stand (in prayer) by night, except a little, half of it, or a little less than that, or add to it, and recite the Qur'an in slow, measured rhythm.﴾ (Surah al-Muzzammil).

This privilege of the Messenger of Allah, although it is an obligation upon him, is not in a mould of iron. Rather, he (ﷺ) has a measure of freedom in this worship; the essential matter is that he stand before Allah for part of the night. But what is the cause of this addition in his case? The cause is in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We are going to send down upon you a heavy word.﴾ (Surah al-Muzzammil). It is as if standing in prayer at night, and standing before Allah at this time, would give the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) the strength and energy necessary to carry this responsibility placed upon his shoulders, namely the responsibility of bearing the method and conveying it to the people.

In the noble hadith: "The Messenger of Allah, whenever a matter distressed him, would rise to prayer." The meaning of ḥazabahu amr (حزبه أمر) is: its causes became too narrow for him and he found no way out of it. If the causes become constricted for him, there is nothing before him but the Causer, exalted is He, to whom he turns and to whose aid he hastens.

﴿Indeed, the rising at night is more effective in tread and more upright in speech.﴾ (Surah al-Muzzammil). Because at the time when people sleep and take their rest, and their heads grow heavy from worship, you stand before your Lord, conversing and humbly supplicating, so mercies and outpourings descend upon you. Whoever among the people rises at this time and follows your example has a share of these mercies and a portion of these outpourings. And whoever's head is too heavy to rise has no share.

Thus: in the night prayer there is faith-strength and spiritual energy. Since the Messenger's task is above the task of the creation, his share of the night prayer is greater than theirs, for the burdens of the Messenger (ﷺ) are many, and a heavy burden needs connection with the One, the Self-Subsisting. So that he may seek help, through meeting his Lord, in fulfilling his affairs.

It is strange that Muslims turn away from this sunnah and neglect it. When a matter distresses them, they do not hasten to prayer; rather they make excuses, and one of them says: "I am busy." Does the busyness of the world justify negligence in this obligation? And who knows, perhaps through prayer doors will be opened for you, and in an hour you will accomplish what you could not accomplish in many days.

We say to those who are lax in prayer and whom worldly affairs distract from it: if they pray, let them pray as a makeshift. If you ask them, they say: "The preoccupations are many and time is not enough." So, if one of them wishes to go to relieve himself, will he find time for this? Undoubtedly he finds time for such a matter, even if the preoccupations of the world assail him. So why is prayer the one for which he finds no time?!

And His saying, Exalted: ﴿As a supererogatory (prayer) for you...﴾ (79) (Surah al-Isra'). Nafilah (النافلة) is what exceeds what is obligated upon everyone. (lak) means: specifically for you, not for others. This is the station of ihsan (excellence) about which Allah said: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and springs, receiving what their Lord has given them. Indeed, they were before that doers of good.﴾ (Surah adh-Dhariyat). The muhsin (doer of good) is one who has entered the station of ihsan, by adding to what Allah obligated upon him, and of the same kind as what was obligated. Therefore the reason for ihsan came:

﴿They used to sleep but little of the night, and in the hours before dawn they would ask forgiveness.﴾ (Surah adh-Dhariyat).

This station is not obligatory upon you. You may pray the isha' and sleep until the dawn prayer. But if you wish to follow the example of the Messenger of Allah and imitate him, then enter the station of ihsan according to your capacity.

Then He, Exalted, says: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station.﴾ (79) (Surah al-Isra'). The verse at its beginning spoke of the obligation, and this is the reward. ʿAsā (عسى) indicates the hope that the action will occur, and there is a difference between tamannī (wishing) and rajāʾ (hoping). Tamannī: you declare that you love something but its occurrence is not possible or is impossible, such as the poet's saying:

"Would that the stars would draw near to me so that I might string them"

The poet wishes that the stars were before him so he could string them into poems of praise for whomever he praises, and this is impossible to happen.

And his saying: "Ah, would that youth returned one day, so I could tell it what old age has done."

As for rajāʾ, it is the request for an action whose occurrence is possible.

Under the heading of request (ṭalab) there are many things. If the speaker requests from the addressee something not possible to occur, it is tamannī; if he requests something possible to occur, it is tarajjī; and if he requests the image of a thing rather than its reality, it is istifhām (interrogation), as you say: "Where is Zayd?" There is a difference between requesting the reality and requesting the image.

If you request the reality of a thing, there are two states before you: either you request the reality as something to be done, and this is a command, such as: "Stand (qum)." Or you request it as something not to be done, and this is a prohibition: "Do not stand (lā taqum)." So ʿasā indicates hope, and it varies according to the one from whom hope is held. If you hope from so-and-so, he may give you or he may fail you. If you say: "ʿAsā an uʿṭiyaka (perhaps I will give you)," you have brought hope close, because I am hoping from myself; but a person by nature is subject to changes, and circumstances may arise so that he does not fulfill what he promised.

If you say: "ʿAsā Allāh an yuʿṭiyaka (perhaps Allah will give you)," this is the strongest hope, because you have hoped from One whom nothing can overpower, nothing is too great for Him, and changes do not touch Him. Thus the hope in it is certain, without doubt.

And al-maqām al-maḥmūd (المقام المحمود): the word maḥmūd means the one upon whom praise falls. Praise here is general, for it does not say "praised by whom?" It is praised by whoever praise can come from: praised by all, from Adam until the Hour.

What is meant by al-maqām al-maḥmūd is the station of intercession, when the creation stands in the courtyard of reckoning, amid the terror and severity of the situation, to the point that people wish to depart even to the Fire. At that moment every nation seeks intercession through its prophet, and they are all turned away until they go to the Seal of the Messengers and Master of the Prophets, and he says: "I am for it, I am for it."

Therefore the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded us to supplicate with this prayer: "And raise him, O Allah, to the praiseworthy station which You have promised him," and there is no doubt that it is a supplication for our own benefit.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 17, verse 80:

Allah's words: ﴿and cause me to enter a sincere entrance﴾ (Surah al-Isra' 17:80). That is, from the general perspective: before you enter, you must first ask for the exit, because you will not enter except after you have exited. Yet the natural order would be to say: "Bring me out with a sincere exit, and bring me in with a sincere entrance."

We say: No, because entering is the goal of exiting, and because exiting is left behind while entering lies ahead for you. Therefore entering is the more important, so it was mentioned first. For this reason they say: "Beware of leaving any matter unless you know how you will enter."

The meaning of a sincere exit (mukhraj al-sidq) and a sincere entrance (mudkhal al-sidq) is that you do not enter or exit without a purpose. If you leave a place, let your exit be a sincere exit, meaning one that corresponds to the reality of your task. If you enter a place, let your entrance be a sincere entrance, meaning for a specific aim you wish to achieve. So if you enter a shop, for example, enter for a purpose, such as buying a commodity; this is a sincere entrance. But if you enter without a purpose, or to harm the creatures of God, there is no sincere entrance in this.

So: let your entering be for Allah and your exiting be for Allah. Thus the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) left Makkah and entered Madinah; his leaving was for Allah and his entering was for Allah. He made a sincere exit and a sincere entrance, because he (ﷺ) did not leave Makkah except when his people harmed him, persecuted him, and fought his call, until the soil of Makkah was no longer suitable for the growth of the call. And he did not enter Madinah except when he saw support and assistance from its people.

Sincerity (al-sidq) means that your conduct and actions correspond to what is in your heart. So there should be no deficiency in your inner intention, and no movement of yours should contradict this aim.

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿and grant me from Yourself an authority (sultan) that helps﴾ (Surah al-Isra' 17:80). This is a request for help from Allah, exalted is He, for His Messenger (ﷺ), because He sent him with the method of truth. This truth will clash with the people of falsehood and corruption, who are eager for falsehood and profit from corruption; these will oppose the call and confront it. Therefore the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned to his Lord, exalted is He, who had sent him, and sought His help in confronting his enemies.

As for His words: ﴿authority that helps﴾ (Surah al-Isra' 17:80): we have previously explained that sultan is meant either as a proof that convinces, or as a sword that deters. This is clear in the words of the Truthful, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs and sent down with them the Scripture and the balance that people may uphold justice﴾ (Surah al-Hadid 57:25). That is, with clear signs, and these are the instruments of proof and persuasion. Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And We sent down iron, wherein is great might and benefits for people﴾ (Surah al-Hadid 57:25). These are the instruments of power and deterrence.

The good among people are restrained by the word of Allah and the word of the Messenger, and they respond. But for the wicked, proof is of no avail; rather, they must be restrained by force. The first, if he is confronted with an oath by Allah, swears truthfully; the other, if he is confronted with an oath, swears falsely, seeing it as an opportunity for escape, and the state of his tongue says: "Relief has come to you."

And it is reported in a narration: "Indeed, Allah restrains by authority what He does not restrain by the Qur'an."

Thus the Truth, glorified be He, launched it as a resounding slogan: "The Truth has come" (jā'a al-ḥaqq). Since He said to the Messenger, "Say" (qul), the Truth must certainly be coming, without any doubt. For this reason He commanded him with this clear command and did not leave him to whisper it to himself. After that, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said it on the year of the Conquest, when he entered Makkah as a conqueror and went around the House, where there were three hundred and sixty idols, and he overturned them all, calling out: "The Truth has come and falsehood has vanished, the Truth has come and falsehood has vanished, for falsehood neither originates nor restores."

That is: the Truth has come and falsehood has been routed, and it no longer has the power by which it could originate or restore. Its strength has been extinguished, and it has no more force or voice left.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Truth has come and falsehood has vanished, surely falsehood is ever bound to vanish﴾ (Surah al-Isra', 81), makes us feel that the Truth came of its own accord, since He attributed the coming to the Truth as though it were an intrinsic quality of it, and no one brought it. Likewise in ﴿and falsehood has vanished﴾ (Surah al-Isra', 81): falsehood by its nature is vanishing, routed, and weak, with no permanence.

It is remarkable that the Truth which came through the hand of the Messenger of Allah at the Conquest of Makkah benefited even those who did not believe. On the day of the Conquest there appears a image of the forms of greatness in the religion of Islam, when the Messenger of Allah gathered the people of Makkah, who had opposed and been arrogant and had expelled the Messenger of Allah from the land most beloved to him. And here he enters it victorious, makes them stand before him, and says: "What do you think I will do with you?" They said: "Good, a noble brother and the son of a noble brother." He said: "Go, for you are free (al-ṭulaqā'), freed ones."

So: the Truth came not to enslave people, but for their comfort and to lift up their heads. Among the Truth that overshadowed Makkah with the Conquest is what is narrated: a man entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ) in the Ka'bah intending to harm him, and when he placed his hand upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), his state changed and he said: "By Allah, I had turned against him, and there was on earth no one more hateful to me than him. But when I placed my hand upon him, by Allah, there was on earth no one more beloved to me than him." Thus the Truth came and falsehood vanished.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, falsehood has ever been vanishing﴾ (Surah al-Isra', 81): zahūq is an intensive form (ṣīghat mubālaghah); falsehood itself swiftly goes away and perishes. And it is remarkable that you see falsehood itself among the soldiers of God, because if falsehood did not pain and disturb people, they would not long for the Truth nor incline toward it. When falsehood stings them and they are burned by its fire, they recognize the Truth.

God, exalted is He, has also set forth for us a parable of the Truth and falsehood, saying: ﴿He sends down water from the sky, and the valleys flow according to their measure, and the torrent carries a swelling foam. And from that which they heat in the fire, seeking an ornament or goods, there is foam like it. Thus God strikes the parables of the Truth and falsehood. As for the foam, it passes away as scum; but as for that which benefits people, it remains in the earth. Thus God strikes parables﴾ (Surah al-Ra'd, 17).

The Truth, glorified be He, illustrates the Truth and falsehood with a sensible thing that we see when rain pours down on the mountain peaks, and the water flows through the valleys between the mountains, carrying with it small pebbles, sand, and chaff. This is the foam that floats on the surface of the water and from which people gain no benefit. When the winds blow, they push this foam aside, and the clear, pure water remains, from which people benefit. This water is an example of the Truth that benefits people, and the foam is an example of falsehood, in which there is no good.

Or: it gives us the example in another form: the image of the blacksmith or goldsmith who kindles fire upon gold to bring out the impurities that cling to it.

The verse presents us with two models of receiving the Qur'an. If the believer receives it, it is for him a healing and a mercy; if the wrongdoer receives it, it brings him only loss. The Qur'an specified "the wrongdoers" to show that their wrongdoing is the cause of their failure to benefit from the Qur'an, because the Qur'an is good in its own essence and is not a loss.

We have already explained that the act may be one, but the recipient of the act differs, and the effect differs from one person to another. Clear water is drunk by the healthy person, who finds in it pleasure and sweetness, while the sick person drinks it and finds it bitter and insipid. The water is one, but the one who is affected by the water differs. Likewise with rich food: when a healthy person eats it, it benefits him and increases his strength and vigor, but when a sick person eats it, it increases his sickness and brings upon him an ailment on top of his ailment.

We have also already explained, in the story of the conversion of al-Faruq ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), that when he received the Qur'an with the spirit of disbelief and obstinacy, he disliked it and shrank from it, and when he received it with the spirit of tenderness, softness and gentleness, toward his sister whose face had been wounded, it pleased him and he believed.

So: the soundness or corruption of one's disposition has an effect on receiving the Qur'an and being moved by it. This matter is similar to the matter of optimism and pessimism. If you have a cup of water that is half full, the optimist's attention is drawn to the full half, whereas the pessimist's attention is drawn to the empty half. The first says: "The cup is half full," and the other says: "The cup is half empty." Both are truthful, but their dispositions differ.

The Qur'an addressed this matter of receiving in His saying, exalted is He:
﴿And when a surah is revealed, among them are some who say, "Which of you has had his faith increased by this?" As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice. And as for those in whose hearts is disease, it has added to them evil upon their evil, and they die while they are disbelievers.﴾ (Surah At-Tawbah).

The verse is one, but the innate disposition is different. The believer receives it with sound faculties, so it increases him in faith; the disbeliever receives it with corrupt faculties, so it increases him in disbelief. Thus, the problem in receiving the truths and taking them in is that the faculties of reception are corrupt.

From here we say: when you look at the truth, beware of looking at it while there is falsehood in your core that you are keen to keep. You must first expel the falsehood you have, then consider and weigh matters. This matter has also come in the saying of Allah, exalted is He:

﴿And among them are those who listen to you, until, when they leave your presence, they say to those who were given knowledge, "What did he just say?" Those are the ones upon whose hearts Allah has set a seal, and they follow their desires. But those who are guided — He increases them in guidance and gives them their righteousness.﴾ (Surah Muhammad).

Their saying "What did he just say?" (Surah Muhammad, 16) is evidence of their lack of concern for the Qur'an, and that it is a thing that is not regarded. Likewise in His saying:
﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an, they would have said, "Why are its verses not explained in detail? Is it a foreign recitation and an Arab [messenger]?" Say: "It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing. And those who do not believe — in their ears is deafness, and it is for them blindness...."﴾ (Surah Fussilat, 44).

An example of sound reception from our contemporary life is the transmission of television, for instance. You may receive it in your home and find it clear in one episode or one program, and you enjoy what you watched. Then you meet a friend who complains of poor reception and unclear picture, and he confirms to you that the transmission is sound. However, the defect is in your receiving device, so you must first adjust your receiving device so that you may receive the signs of Allah with correct reception.

So: the saying of the Truth, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers...﴾ (Surah Al-Isra, 82) depends on the soundness of disposition, the soundness of reception, and the understanding of what comes from Allah, exalted is He.

Healing is that you treat an existing disease so that you are cured of it. Mercy is that you take preventive measures that guarantee you will not relapse into the illness again. So mercy is prevention, and healing is treatment.

But is the healing of the Qur'an a spiritual healing for the diseases of the hearts and ailments of the souls, so that the Muslim is freed from anxiety, confusion and jealousy, and uproots what is in himself of rancor, hatred and envy, and other spiritual diseases? Or is it a healing for material things and for bodily diseases as well?

The preponderant opinion, indeed the certain one about which there is no doubt, is that the Qur'an is a healing in the general, comprehensive sense of this word. It is a healing for material things just as it is a healing for spiritual things, as evidenced by what is narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him), that he went out at the head of a military detachment. They passed by a people and asked them for food, but they refused to feed them. It happened that the chief of the people was stung by a scorpion, and they needed someone to treat him, so they asked for someone to perform ruqyah on him. They said: "We will not perform ruqyah on him except for a reward," because of what they had seen of their stinginess and their failure to honor them, in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken for it a payment.﴾ (Surah Al-Kahf, 77).

When they agreed with them on a reward of food and sheep, one of them performed ruqyah on the stung man with Surah al-Fatihah, and he was healed. They ate of the food and left the sheep, until they returned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him about the permissibility of this reward. He (ﷺ) said: "And how did you know it was a ruqyah?" meaning: it is a ruqyah by which the patient is treated and recovers by the permission of Allah. Then he (ﷺ) said: "Eat of it, and set aside a share for me with you."

So the healing of bodily diseases is something present in the Sunnah, and it is not a wonder of the wonders, because when you read the speech of Allah, know that the One speaking these words is the Truth, glorified is He, the Lord and Sovereign of everything, who disposes of His dominion as He wills, and by the word "Be" He does what He wishes. It is not far-fetched that the speech of Allah should affect the patient so that he is healed. When some objectors debated this matter with one of the scholars, they said to him: "How can a patient be healed by a word? This is not reasonable." The scholar said to his companion: "Be silent, you donkey!" The man became angry and was about to leave the place, his fury aroused. The scholar looked at him and said: "See what a word has done to you. So what of a word whose speaker is Allah, glorified and exalted?"

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss.﴾ (Surah Al-Isra, 82). This is because, by their wrongdoing and their reception of the outpourings of heaven with sickly faculties and conflicting, opposed devices, they gained nothing from the Qur'an and did not benefit from the mercies of Allah.

Allah, exalted is He, wants to give man a picture of himself, so that he has sufficient immunity when illness strikes him, just as the doctor gives the dose of vaccine or inoculation that prevents a particular disease from occurring. This is man's nature and his dominant characteristic, and he must work to moderate this nature. The meaning is that when Allah bestows His blessing upon man, he becomes self-sufficient and turns away.

To clarify this matter, we give an example, and to Allah belongs the highest likeness: a father who gives his son his allowance each month, for instance. You see the boy does not pay attention to his father except at the beginning of each month, when the time arrives for the allowance he is accustomed to receive, and you see him throughout the month turned away from his father, scarcely remembering him. But if he accustoms him to giving his allowance every day, you see the boy in the morning approaching his father and presenting himself before him to remind him of what is due. So when the son turned away from his father and departed from him, what was it that prompted this behaviour?

It is because the father gave him the capacity to be independent of him throughout the month. If the son is dutiful and believing, he does not forget his father's favour, who provided him with this capacity for independence, so he mentions his father with goodness and acknowledges this kindness. If this is the case with the lower Lord, it is likewise with the Higher Lord, glory be to Him. He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And when We bestow favour upon man, he turns away...﴾ [17:83]. That is: he turns away from Us and from our remembrance, and departs from Our way.
