As for a name of active attribute, it has an opposite: "al-Mu'izz" (the Exalter) is an active attribute, meaning He exalts others, and its opposite is "al-Mudhill" (the Abaser); "al-Darr" (the Harmful) has as its opposite "al-Nafi'" (the Beneficial); "al-Muhyi" (the Giver of Life) has as its opposite "al-Mumit" (the Causer of Death), and so on. If you find an opposite for a name, know that it is a name of an active attribute of God the Exalted; and if it has no opposite, it is a name of essence.

But you stop, for example, at "al-Sattar" (the Concealer), which is an active attribute because He conceals others, but it has no opposite; we do not say "al-Fada!" (the Exposer). Why? Because He, blessed and exalted, wants His creatures to take on this attribute, and He wants the attribute of concealment to be instilled in people toward one another. If people knew about someone a shameful matter, they would renounce everything that comes from him, even if it were good, and thus society would be deprived of many energies of goodness.

But when you conceal the flaw of one with a flaw, you give society the opportunity to benefit from what he possesses of good qualities. Therefore God, the Exalted, when His servant disobeys, loves to conceal him, so that the wheel of life may continue; for there is no one who has perfection except the Prophet (ﷺ), and the poet spoke truly:

"Who is there who has never erred, and who has only the Most Beautiful (attributes)?"

So: it is part of wisdom that God, the Exalted, commands the concealment of the unseen faults of His creatures from one another, so that the movement of life continues; for man is a son of changing states, and his heart quickly turns, and perhaps if you knew something hidden about him, you would change toward him, and he likewise toward you, and perhaps the ties of affection between us would be cut; but through concealment each of us benefits from the other.

From here they said: "If you were to expose one another, you would not bury one another," meaning: if secrets were uncovered and each of you knew the flaw of his brother, you would not bury any of you who died; and this is the extreme of what can be imagined of severance among people.

As for His saying, exalted is He: "Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful; whichever you call upon, to Him belong the Most Beautiful Names" (Surah al-Isra', 110). He chose this name specifically: (Allah), the proper name for the Necessarily Existent, which is a name of essence that does not indicate a specific attribute, but it carries within it all the attributes of perfection. Though the other names have their fields, the Powerful in power, the Wise in wisdom, the Restrainer in restraint, the Mighty in might, each name has its domain and its flow; (Allah) is the name that comprises all attributes.

Therefore, in the noble prophetic hadith: "Every matter not begun with the name of Allah is cut off (abtar)."

Why? Because when you undertake any action, you first need wisdom to know through it why you are doing it, you need power to help you accomplish it, and you need knowledge of the outcome and consequence of this action. So: you need many attributes. When you set about work, do not say "O Wise, O Powerful, O Knowing"; rather, the Truth, glorified is He, eases you, and it suffices that you say at the beginning of the action: "In the name of Allah," because you have mentioned the name that comprises all attributes of perfection.

"Or call upon the Most Merciful" (Surah al-Isra', 110). He chose al-Rahman rather than al-Jabbar or al-Qahhar, because mercy is the attribute of tenderness toward creatures; the Truth, glorified and exalted, manifests this attribute to His servants even in the names al-Jabbar and al-Qahhar, because they serve mercy and are among its causes; for when the servant knows of God the attribute of majesty, the attribute of subjugation, and the attribute of retribution, he refrains from the causes of falling under the reach of these attributes, so it is as if He shows mercy to His servants even through the attributes of subjugation and retribution.

From this is the saying of the Truth, blessed and exalted: "And in retaliation there is life for you, O people of understanding" (Surah al-Baqarah, 179); for when the killer knows he will be killed, he refrains from killing. And in the report: "Killing is the surest deterrent to killing."

So: the legislation of retaliation and the establishment of prescribed punishments and penalties is not to torment creatures, but is mercy toward them, so that they stand far from committing what requires retaliation, prescribed punishment, or penalty. Even the one whom God subjugates is also shown mercy; for as long as He has said: "I am the Subjugator, so beware of Me," He thereby shows mercy to him, because He warns him of the causes of falling into what merits His anger and retribution.

Likewise, He chose the name al-Rahman because the whole field of obligation is mercy; the method was revealed from God only to regulate people's lives and to achieve for them happiness in the movement of life, so that creation completes itself among themselves, cooperates, supports one another and does not oppose one another, and they all stand as one man's heart. This is the aim of the divine method in the world of people: that the Muslim society live secure and safe.

Thus divine Compassionateness (al-rahmaniyya) is predominant in all legislation, and it is the general characteristic; do you not see His saying, exalted is He: "The Most Merciful. (1) Taught the Qur'an. (2)" (Surah al-Rahman).

The Qur'an, which was revealed to regulate and govern people's lives, to set right the movement of life, and to establish peace between you and God, between you and yourself, and between you and others, this Qur'an is a manifestation of this divine Compassionateness.

Some orientalists objected to His saying in Surah al-Rahman: "Then which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny? (13)" (Surah al-Rahman), where "ala'" (favours) means blessings; and that it came as a concluding remark to His saying: "A flame of fire and molten brass will be sent against you both, and you will not be able to defend yourselves (35)" (Surah al-Rahman). The verse speaks of fire and flame, so how does it end with this conclusion that indicates blessing?

Had these people reflected, they would not have objected; for in warning against it and frightening with it there is a blessing. It is as if the Qur'an says to you: beware of doing what requires the fire and flame, so that you withdraw and refrain in time. Is this not one of God's blessings upon His servants? Is it not mercy toward them? And what would you have said if the Truth, glorified is He, had not given you a warning and admonition, and then surprised you with punishment?

We stop at another subtlety in the use of the name Allah's (al-Rahman) in His saying: "Then He istawa (rose) over the Throne, the Most Merciful; ask about Him one who is informed (59)" (Surah al-Furqan). That is: after He created creation, each with its heavens and earth and what is in them, He istawa over the Throne; because istiwa' over the Throne means that everything has been completed for Him, glorified is He, in creation and origination, and it ended in sitting upon the Throne. This is an analogy with kings, who do not sit upon the throne until their affair is firmly established for them; the king's sitting on the throne means that he is the one unique who is not opposed by anyone.

So the Truth, glorified is He, alerts us by His saying: "Then He istawa over the Throne, the Most Merciful" (Surah al-Furqan, 59). He chose the attribute of mercy to suggest to us that His sitting on the Throne does not mean subjugation and tyranny; rather, He sat upon His Throne out of mercy toward you, sat upon the Throne to regulate your lives and have some of you show mercy to others, so that you may be happy in life. So the istiwa' here is not istiwa' of subjugation and domination, but istiwa' of mercy for your own benefit.

In another verse He said: "The Most Merciful istawa over the Throne" (Surah Taha, 5). His istiwa' over the Throne has been mentioned in seven places in the Book of God, which a versifier arranged in his saying:

"And the mention of God's istiwa' in His words over the Throne, in seven places, so count them.
In Surah al-A'raf, then Yunus, and in al-Ra'd with Taha, so for counting they have stipulated.
In Surah al-Furqan, then the prostration, likewise in al-Hadid; understand, understanding confirmed."

And every attribute of His majesty, glorified is He, is in the service of His compassionateness, for He frightens His servants with attributes of majesty so that they do not fall into disobedience, and so they receive God's blessing in this world and are happy with it, and receive the bliss of the Hereafter and are happy with it. So it is the all-dominant compassionateness and the general characteristic of God's method in this world and the next.

In the hadith: "On the last night of Ramadan, al-Jabbar manifests Himself with forgiveness..." and he did not say "al-Ghaffar manifests Himself with forgiveness," so why did he prefer the attribute al-Jabbar in the field of forgiveness?

They said: because forgiveness suggests the existence of a sin, and sin requires punishment, and this belongs to the attribute al-Jabbar. Has the attribute al-Ghaffar overcome the attribute al-Jabbar and taken over its domain? No; rather the attribute al-Ghaffar intercedes with the attribute al-Jabbar: "The decision is yours, O attribute; but we ask your pardon to intercede for these people." So the attributes of beauty intercede with the attributes of majesty.

Therefore, those who interpret the hadith say: the believers interceded, the prophets interceded, the angels interceded, and there remained the intercession of the Most Merciful of the merciful. To whom will the Most Merciful of the merciful intercede? They said: His essence intercedes with His essence; and thus the attribute of beauty (al-Ghaffar) intercedes with the attribute of majesty (al-Jabbar), blessed and exalted.

Then He, exalted, says: "Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful; whichever you call upon, to Him belong the Most Beautiful Names" (Surah al-Isra', 110).

So whichever name you call upon Him by, since all His names are beautiful; but let there be intelligence in your supplication, so that you call upon Him with what suits your need. If you want knowledge, say: "O Knower, teach me"; if you are weak, say: "O Strong, strengthen me"; if you want honour, say: "O Mighty, honour me," and so on. If you want brevity, say: "O Allah"; it suffices you for everything.

Then He, exalted, says: "And do not recite your prayer aloud, nor be silent therein, but seek a way between those" (Surah al-Isra', 110).

Prayer here is meant to include all acts of prayer. (Wa la tajhar) "And do not recite aloud": loudness is forbidden; likewise (wa la tukhafit) "nor be silent," that is, do not make it so quiet that it cannot be heard by

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 17, verse 111:

So what is praised in the verse?

God, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Who has not taken a son...﴾ (111) (Surat al-Isra'). His not having taken a son is a great blessing upon the servants, for which they must praise Him. If He had a son, He would single him out with His care to the exclusion of the rest of creation. He, glory be to Him, is exalted above having a son, and He has made all creation His dependants, and they are all equal before Him. There is none among them who is a son of God, or who has kinship with God. The most beloved of them to Him, exalted be He, is the most God-fearing. In this way, creation alone enjoys all the tenderness of their Lord and all His mercy.

Then, what is the wisdom behind taking a son? People take sons and are eager for offspring, especially for two reasons: so that the son may be a remembrance and an extension of his father after his death, as the poet said:

"My son, I am the one who, after I have died..."

But God, glory be to Him, is eternal and everlasting, so He has no need of someone to perpetuate His remembrance or to be an extension of Him. Exalted is God above that, with a great exaltation. So praise be to God that He has not taken a son.

Or a son may be for support and for numbers, and for strength against weakness. God, glory be to Him, is the Victorious, the Subduer, so He has no need of support or multitude. Therefore He commands us to glorify Him because He has not taken a companion or a son. Whoever reflects on the state of kings and sultans will find that most of their corruption comes either from sons or from wives.

Then He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And He has no partner in the dominion...﴾ (111) (Surat al-Isra').

This too is among the blessings that call for praise. And you may imagine: if God had a partner in dominion, how bewildered the servants would be. Which of them would you obey, and which would you please?

The Truth, glory be to Him, has clarified this matter in the parable He has struck for us: ﴿God presents an example: a man in whom are partners at odds with one another, and a man belonging entirely to one man. Are they equal in comparison?﴾ (29) (Surat al-Zumar).

Therefore, in the customs and proverbs of people they say: "The boat that has two captains sinks." His being one, without partner, makes you content with His command and prohibition, so you obey Him while at peace. His commands are binding, with none to reverse them and none to object to them. There is no other god who commands you to something contrary. Is this not a blessing that calls for praise?

Also, God, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And He has no protector out of weakness...﴾ (111) (Surat al-Isra').

The wali (protector) is the one who stands in charge of you. You do not entrust your affairs except to one whom you trust to bring you benefit, or to ward off harm from you, or to support you against an enemy, or to strengthen your weakness. If you have no self-sufficiency by which to achieve what you want, you turn to one who has self-sufficiency, and you seek refuge in his protection, and you give your loyalty to him.

God, glory be to Him, has no protector who seeks Him so that He may exalt him, because He, glory be to Him, is the Mighty, the Giver of might, who subsists in His own essence, and He has no need of anyone. Then He, exalted be He, says: ﴿And magnify Him with magnification...﴾ (111) (Surat al-Isra'). Because the greatness of God, glory be to Him, in the heart of the believer is greater than everything and greater than every great thing. For this reason, "God is greatest" (Allahu akbar) has been made the emblem of your call to prayer and of your prayer. So you must magnify God and make Him greater than whatever else is among the transient things. If He calls you while you are at any work, say: "God is greater than my work." And if He calls you while you are in the presence of a great person, say: "God is greater than any great one." Magnify Him with magnification by giving precedence to His commands and prohibitions over every command and every prohibition.

Do not forget that if you magnify the Truth, glory be to Him, you will honour yourself with the honour of God, which He bestows only upon those who sincerely devote themselves to His servitude, glory be to Him. Furthermore, servitude to God is an honour for the servant, and through it the servant receives the best of his Master. As for servitude to human beings, it is blameworthy and detestable, and it is humiliation and abasement, since the master takes the best of his servant.

The poet spoke truly when he said:

"It is enough honour for my soul that I am a servant
Who welcomes me without appointments with my Lord.
He is in His holiness the Most Mighty, but
I meet Him whenever and wherever I love."

How much hardship and difficulty you endure in meeting a great one among the great men of this world! But in meeting the Lord of Might, glory be to Him, the moment you have believed in Him, the reins are in your hand: you meet Him whenever you wish, in whatever place you desire, and you speak with Him about whatever matter you love. So what honour is there after this?

For this reason, the ground of elevation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the Isra' and Mi'raj was that he was a servant of God, as He said: ﴿Glory be to the One who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque...﴾ (1) (Surat al-Isra').

So honour lies in servitude to God, and honour lies in prostration to Him, exalted be He. Your servitude to God protects you from servitude to other than Him, and your prostration to Him protects you from prostration to other than Him. Do you not see the poet's words:

"And the prostration that you find distasteful
Among a thousand prostrations is salvation in it."

So then: magnify God with magnification and greatness, and take refuge in Him. Whoever takes refuge in God, exalted be He, is in His companionship, and the Truth pours upon him from His attributes and protects him from the plots of others and their subjugation. We previously gave an example of the young child who is attacked by his peers if he walks alone, but if he is in his father's hand, no one dares to attack him.

So it is incumbent upon you always to be in the companionship of your Lord, so that you are safe from the plots of the plotters and the schemes of the schemers, and no one may harm you. If God tests him with something, it is as though He says to him: "I test you with My blessing so that you may take from My essence, because the healthy and well person, if he is in the companionship of God's blessing, then the afflicted one is in the companionship of God Himself."

Did the Truth, glory be to Him, not say in the hadith qudsi: "O son of Adam, I was sick and you did not visit Me." He says: "O Lord, how could I visit You, when You are the Lord of the worlds?" He says: "Did you not know that My servant so-and-so was sick and you did not visit him? Did you not know that if you had visited him, you would have found Me with him?"

The sick person who is comforted by his visitors, delights in them, and sees in their visits a lightening of his pains and consolation in his hardship: what then of one who finds comfort in God and is in His neighbourhood and His protection? By God, there is no god but He, he does not feel the sting of illness at all, and he is ashamed to groan from pain, and he does not despair however severe the trial becomes upon him, because how could he groan from the companionship of God? And how could he despair while God, the Exalted, is with him?

So then: magnify Him with magnification. That is: make His command and prohibition above everything, and say: "God is greater than every great thing, even Paradise. Say: God is greater than Paradise." Do you not see the words of Rabi'a al-'Adawiyya:

"They all worship You out of fear of the Fire,
Or that they may dwell in the gardens and be favoured,
As for me, I have no share in the gardens or the Fire,
They regard salvation as a generous share,
In palaces, and drinking from Salsabil.
I do not seek any substitute for my love."

And in the hadith qudsi: "Had I not created Paradise and Fire, would I not be worthy to be worshipped?"

So God, glory be to Him in His essence, is greater than anything, even if it be Paradise. In the last surah of al-Kahf, He, exalted be He, says: ﴿Whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous work and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord.﴾ (110) (Surat al-Kahf).

He did not say: "Whoever hopes for the reward of his Lord, or the Paradise of his Lord, or the bounties of his Lord." The true believer does not look to the bounty; rather, he longs for the meeting with the Bestower, glory be to Him, and this is the ultimate of his hopes.

In another hadith, the Truth, glory be to Him, says to the angels: "Have you not seen My servants? I have bestowed upon them such and such, and I withhold My blessing from them, and yet they love Me."

With this verse Surat al-Isra' is concluded. God, the Truth, has made us conclude it with mention of these three blessings He has bestowed upon us. These are not all of God's blessings upon us; rather, God has upon us blessings that cannot be counted or enumerated, but these three are the pinnacle of the blessings that call for us to praise Him for them.

So praise be to God who has not taken a son, because He does not beget and was not begotten, and He is One, the Unique. Praise be to God who has not taken a partner, because He is One. Praise be to God who has had no protector out of weakness, because He is the Dominant, the Mighty, the Giver of might. For this reason we must magnify this God with magnification in every blessing we receive from Him, glory be to Him.
